translations.text: The Life of Vakhtang Gorgasali: of his parents, and after that of the great and God-loving king himself,
who proved more renowned than all the kings of Kartli. How the Persians captured Mirdat, king of the Georgians, in battle and took him away to Baghdad, and he died there.
The Persians seized Kartli, ruined the churches, and the Georgians hid their crosses.
In all the churches of Kartli the fire-worshipping Persians kindled fire. But the kinsmen of the Georgian kings remained in the valley of Kakheti.
Three years later the king of the Persians had no time to spare, because enemies had risen against him in the east.

Then the nobles of Kartli made an agreement among themselves. They brought the son of Trdat, the nephew of Mirdat, the king who had been carried off captive, whose name was Archil, and set him up as king in Mtskheta.
The thirty-first king, Archil, son of King Mirdat.
This Archil the Khosroid brought a wife from Greece, a kinswoman of King Jovian, named Mariam, and declared hostility to the Persians.
He brought the crosses out into the open and adorned the churches. He slaughtered all the fire-worshippers and drove them out of the borders of Kartli.
He gathered forces from Greece and, with the cross going before him, began to make war on the Persians.
At that time there was an eristavi of the Persian king who governed Ran and Movakan. Until Archil's reign, Kartli too had been under his administration.
He gathered the army of Ran, Movakan and Adarbadagan and marched against Archil.
But Archil, hoping and trusting in God, went to meet him on the border between Kartli and Ran, and drew up for battle there on the river Berduji.
By the power of the venerable cross he slaughtered them and took them captive. He went into Ran, plundered it, and came home victorious.
He sent out a herald through all of Kartli and said to everyone: "It was not by our own strength, nor by courage, nor by wisdom, nor by the number of our troops that we defeated our enemies,
but by the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who gave us his venerable cross as our leader and our weapon.
Now, all you Georgians, glorify the consubstantial Trinity, God without beginning, Creator of all things.
Offer thanks, and may your hearts be firm in the faith of the Holy Trinity."
All the Georgians offered thanks to God and renewed the churches.
Then King Archil built the church of Saint Stephen in Mtskheta, at the Aragvi gates, where there were strong fortified towers that he had also built.
A son was born to Archil, and he named him Mirdat. This Mirdat grew up and reached manhood. Mirdat was a believer and a servant of God, like
his father. He was also bold and enterprising. More than his father, he began to make war on the Persians, to invade Ran and Movakan and to plunder them.
At that time the king of the Persians had no time to spare: he was fighting the Indians, the Sindians and the Abyssinians, and he could not send a large army.
And the Georgians were getting the better of the armies of Ran, Movakan and Adarbadagan.
Mirdat would lead his father's troops, and he constantly raided Ran and Movakan.
At that time Barzabod was eristavi (duke) of Ran. He was never able to stand against him, but instead fortified his fortresses and cities.
And when the Georgians entered Ran, wherever the Persians met the plundering Georgians with the remnants of their armies, the Persians were always defeated.
Now Barzabod, the eristavi of Ran, had a daughter, well-formed and beautiful, whose name was Sagdukht.
They told Mirdat, son of Archil, about her beauty, and from hearing of her beauty Mirdat fell in love with her.
He petitioned his father: "I beseech your majesty: bring me Sagdukht, the daughter of Barzabod, as my wife, and let us make peace between us.
Although by the power of Christ we are victorious, we still cannot take the fortresses and cities of Ran.
Let it not happen that the king of the Persians finds leisure and takes revenge on us, and that they lay waste our churches and our borders.
So now let the enmity between us be ended by this. For whatever I petition the king of the Persians on our behalf, he will listen.
By this we will hold the borders of Kartli firmly and unshakably, and the faith of Christ will be strengthened in Kartli,
and doubt and blasphemy against the faith of Christ will no longer arise in the hearts of the Georgians because of the oppression of the Persians." Mirdat said all this out of love for the girl.
Then King Archil fulfilled his wish. He sent an envoy to Barzabod and asked for his daughter as a wife for his son.
Barzabod rejoiced with great joy, because his land had been laid waste and was in distress. He asked for an oath and a promise of peace, and they gave him the oath.
And he gave his daughter with a large dowry. They brought her to Mtskheta and held the wedding, with feasting and rejoicing for many days.
The king gave Samshvilde, together with its eristavate, to his son, and Mirdat and Sagdukht settled there.
This Queen Sagdukht inquired into the faith of Christ, for her husband brought her men learned in the faith, and they explained to her the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ.
And they showed her that Christ is the true God, who became man for our salvation.
Then Sagdukht understood and recognized the true faith. She abandoned fire-worship, was baptized, and became a believer.
And she built the Sioni of Samshvilde. In the time of this Archil three bishops died: Jonah, Gregory, and Basil.
After Basil, this same Archil appointed a bishop named Mobidan. He was Persian by birth, and he made a show of Orthodoxy.
But he was a lawless magus and a corrupter of the rules of the faith. King Archil and his son did not perceive Mobidan's impiety, but thought him a believer.
He did not dare to preach his doctrine openly, out of fear of the king and the people, but secretly he wrote books full of every kind of deception.
After his time, all his writings were burned by the true bishop Michael, who was deposed for his affront to King Vakhtang.
This King Archil spent all the days of his life in the faith of the Holy Trinity
and in building churches. Throughout Kartli he increased the number of priests, deacons, and servants of the churches. Then he died.
The thirty-second king: Mirdat, son of King Archil, a Khosroid. His son Mirdat sat as king in his place, and he reigned like his father, in great faith.
Queen Sagdukht conceived and bore a daughter, and she named her Khuarandze.
Again King Mirdat and Queen Sagdukht prayed to God to give them a son. And after four years Sagdukht conceived and bore a son,
and she named him in Persian Varan-Khuasro-Tang, but in Georgian he was called Vakhtang.
His parents were filled with joy at the birth of this child Vakhtang, and they sent messengers with the good news to all the eristavs.
And they brought out a great treasure, gold and silver, and distributed it to the poor, and they offered thanks to God with prayer and night vigils for many days.
And after this the king summoned all the nobles to the city;
and for many days he held feasting and celebration, and all prayed to God for the upbringing of the child Vakhtang.
The spaspet Saurmag asked the king, with great entreaty, for Vakhtang to foster, and the king granted it and gave his son Vakhtang to the spaspet Saurmag to foster.
For it was the custom that the children of kings were brought up in the houses of the nobles.
After this, in the sixth year, Sagdukht bore another daughter, and she named her Mirandukht.
And the spasalar of Kaspi asked for her to foster, and the king gave her to him; and he took her to the city of Kaspi, and she was brought up there.
In the second year after this King Mirdat died; and Vakhtang was left a child of seven years.
The thirty-third king, Vakhtang, son of Mirdat, a Khosroid. Then Queen Sagdukht, troubled about her father Barzabod,
[thought:] "May my father not bear a grudge over what my father-in-law and my husband did, by which so many evils came upon him, and may he not bear a grudge against me for my abandoning the faith,
and destroy my son, ruin Kartli, and destroy the faith of Christ" — all this she considered, and she fell into great sorrow.
She prayed to God and resolved to go before her father and fall down before him.
She brought together all the eristavs with the spaspet, and with bitter tears she entrusted her son to the spaspet and all the eristavs.
And she went to Bardav to her father. She uncovered her head, knelt down, bared her breasts, fell on her face and laid her face upon his feet;
she bathed her father's feet with tears and begged him for mercy, and that he not remember the deeds of her father-in-law and her husband, and for forgiveness for her abandoning the faith.
And she begged him not to force her to abandon the faith of Christ, for he is the true God.
And she begged him to keep her son in his patrimony and to be his protector before the king of the Persians.
Then Barzabod, who had been prepared to do evil to the Georgians, took pity on his daughter:
He did not force them to abandon their faith, and he granted all his requests; but concerning the faith he said this:
"I will not force any Georgian, or anyone else, to abandon the faith of Christ,
but I will send fire-worshippers to your city, and bishops of our faith will be there over them. And whatever Georgian
chooses our faith of his own free will, do not hinder him."
Then Sagdukht obeyed her father out of great fear. She gave her promise, trusting in God, and came to Kartli.
Then Barzabod sent fire-worshippers to Mtskheta, with Binkaran as their bishop, and they settled at Moguta.
Queen Sagdukht governed the kingdom with the power and help of her father.
Barzabod, Sagdukht's father, died, and in his place the king of the Persians appointed his son Varaz-Bakur, the brother of Queen Sagdukht.
Saurmag the spaspet, Vakhtang's foster-father, died. Then the king appointed another spaspet, whose name was Juansher.
Binkaran, the bishop of the fire-worshippers, taught the Georgians his religion. None of the nobles obeyed him, but many of the common people turned to fire-worship.
Fire-worship became mixed in among the common people of Kartli. Queen Sagdukht grieved over this, but because of the oppression of the Persians she dared do nothing.
Then she brought a true priest from Greece, named Michael, and appointed him bishop of the Upper Church,
for Bishop Mobidan had died. This Bishop Michael opposed Binkaran the deceiver, for he taught all the Georgians the true faith.
He kept all the nobles of Kartli and most of the people in the faith, but a few of the common people turned to fire-worship.
When Vakhtang was ten years old, the Ossetians came down with countless troops and plundered Kartli from the head of the Kura as far as Khunani.
They laid waste the plains, but the fortresses and towns held out against them, except Kaspi.
They destroyed the town of Kaspi and took its people captive, and they carried off Vakhtang's sister Mirandukht, a three-year-old girl. Which [?]
The valleys of Kartli, together with Kakheti, Klarjeti and Egrisi, were left unplundered by them. They went down into Ran and Movakan,
plundered those lands as well, and passed through the Gate of Derbent, for the people of Derbent themselves let them through. They returned victorious to Ossetia.
At the same time the Greeks came out of Abkhazia, for the Greeks held the whole region below the Egris-tsqali. They seized the land from the Egris-tsqali as far as the fortress of Goji (Tsikhegoji).
Then there was mourning and grief among all the Georgians, and they said:
"We have sinned greatly against God, and we have not kept well the faith of Christ and the rule of John's commandment.

"God has justly brought this wrath upon us. He has handed us over to be plundered by foreign peoples, and he has let the Greeks take our borderland from us, just as he took Klarjeti from King Varaz-Bakar.
"That happened because of Varaz-Bakar's sin, for he did not keep the law of Christ well.
"But this has not happened because of our kings' sin. It has happened because of the sins of the people. Our king is now a child,
"and we have no leader to lead us with hope in Christ and under the leadership of the Cross.
"Let us take vengeance on the Ossetians first, and afterwards let us seek to recover the borderland of Kartli from the Greeks."
All the Georgians said this, and they were in great grief.
Meanwhile Vakhtang was growing up and learning every commandment of the Lord from Bishop Michael. From the days of his childhood he loved the law of Christ more than any of the kings of Kartli.
He grieved because fire-worship had crept into Kartli, and because of the captivity and the seizure of the borderlands.
In his mind he was all the more zealous for the Law, but because of the tyranny of the Persians he did not dare to show it openly.
Then, when Vakhtang was fifteen years old, he summoned all the nobles of Kartli and gathered them all in the city.
The king had a hall made ready and sat on a high throne, and Juansher the spaspet and both bishops also sat on thrones,
and all the other eristavis sat on seats, while the commanders of thousands, the commanders of hundreds and all the people stood. Then the king,
like an old and wise man, and as one brought up among philosophers, began to speak in a loud voice and said:
"Trial and affliction come upon kings and peoples from God because of their sins: when believers fall short in the service of God and transgress the commandment,
he brings upon them afflictions such as this one that has now come upon us, just as a good father trains his son well in good deeds.
And if the son does not carry out his father's teaching well, the father punishes him with beatings and instruction, so that he may learn every good thing and become fit for good.
In the same way God, the creator of heaven and earth, has chastised us.
Therefore we must give thanks for his mercies." Then all gave thanks to God.
Again King Vakhtang began to speak and said to all the nobles: "Hear my voice.
Although I am a youth and you have seen no good from me, you have seen great benefits and honours from my fathers, you who have been appointed to positions of rule.
Now, if God keeps us alive, benefits and honours will come to you such as you never saw from my fathers.
Now this is what I say to you: although this trial has come equally upon me and upon you,
regard it as though it had not come upon you, but upon me alone.
And let there be no thought in my heart that those upon whom the trials came are doing this for the sake of their own vengeance.
Rather, I will count you all as serving me, and I will repay you with good for everything.
I will not endure the scorn of the Ossetians. Instead, with hope and trust in God, the consubstantial and unoriginate Trinity,
and with the precious Cross going before us, which has been given as guide and weapon to those who revere him with their hearts,
let us take vengeance on the Ossetians. If this had been inflicted on us by the kings of the Persians or by the king of the Greeks, we would have endured it.
But since it has come upon us from the contemptible Ossetians, it is not right to endure it: death is better for us."
Then Juansher the spaspet rose and said: "Live forever in glory, O king, and may your will be done against your enemies.
You have spoken the truth: this trial has come upon us because of our sins, and God has judged us justly, for we multiplied sin before him.
And it is right for us to give thanks to God, for we deserved great punishment, not one as small as the one that has come upon us.
The All-merciful did not repay us with a punishment as great as our sins, but chastised us with this small punishment.
And for this we, the inhabitants of Kartli, owe great thanks to God.
For you, better than all the kings of Kartli and greater than your fathers, perfect in every way,
like the giant Nimrod, he has raised up as a leader for us, and you have been given by God to put an end to our troubles,
old and new. And if our sins do not prevail,
we expect through you an end to all our troubles and a greater expansion of our borders than at any time, for none of our fathers has been like you.
Live forever, O king! Since this has come upon us from the Ossetians, for these five years we have been in great sorrow,
because you were a child and did not have the strength for warfare and for leading in battle, nor yet for governing the kingdom at home.
Now, O king, although you are perfect in wisdom and strength, in courage and stature, you still lack full age for warfare.
Yet I see your wisdom: although you are a youth, you are able to govern the kingdom, but it is not yet the time for you to wage war and to draw up battle lines.
This is my counsel: that by your wisdom and by consulting your mother you choose one of us as leader of our army,
and give all of us to him, and let us be obedient to him as to your father, and by the power of the Trinity, God of one essence, let us go forth and seek vengeance.
But you, stay at home and govern the kingdom. If because of our sins we are defeated by the Ossetians, your kingdom will remain unharmed;
but if, on the other hand, you yourself are defeated because of our sins, our land will perish utterly, for there is no one to take your place on earth."
This is what Juansher the spaspet (commander-in-chief) said, and all the nobles and eristavis (dukes) agreed with his advice. Then the king said:
"As befits your perfect wisdom and loyalty, so you have set everything out, Juansher; but I do not submit to the advice
that counsel of yours, for since that trial came upon us, all the days of my life I have spent in sorrow, like one living in darkness.
And pity for my sister consumes my heart like a sword of fire, and I would rather choose death for myself than life.
But trusting in God and with the precious Cross leading the way, I will go in person, and I hope in his great mercies that he will not forsake me and will give me victory."
Then, since they could no longer dissuade him, all those nobles agreed and said: "Live forever, O king!
Let your plan be carried out; may God the Creator send his angel to be your strength, and may he strike down all your enemies and establish your kingdom."
[Heading:] Preparation of the campaign against Ossetia. And they confirmed the campaign against Ossetia, and they all dispersed, each to his own home, to make preparations.
And King Vakhtang sent an envoy to his mother's brother, Varaz-Bakur, eristavi (duke) of Ran:
he informed him of the campaign against Ossetia and asked him for help. And he promised it with joy, for his own land too had been taken captive by the Ossetians.
And Vakhtang summoned all the troops of Kartli; and they all assembled and encamped at Mukhnari and Kherki, on this side and that of the Aragvi:
and there were one hundred thousand horsemen and sixty thousand foot soldiers; and Varaz-Bakur sent his own troops, twelve thousand horsemen.
And King Vakhtang went out from the city of Mtskheta, and mustered in full

his troops and reviewed them. Their numbers, the quality of their horses and their equipment pleased him, and he saw that all of them were cheerful and eager [?], for they were full [?] of hatred for the Ossetians.
He was filled with joy and gave thanks to God. He went into the city and spent one week in prayer, fasting and night vigils, and he gave out a great amount of treasure to the poor.
And he left his mother Sagdukht and his sister Khuarandze to govern his kingdom, and he wrote a testament as follows:
"If I do not come back alive, let my sister Khuarandze marry Mirian," who was Vakhtang's first cousin, the son of his father's brother,
"of the lineage of Rev, son of Mirian, who was the son-in-law of Trdat, king of the Armenians. Let him marry my sister, and let him hold the kingship."
He gave this document to his mother and told no one else. And he left that Mirian, his paternal first cousin, in Mtskheta.
Vakhtang set out and halted at Tianeti. There all the kings of the Caucasus joined him, with fifty thousand horsemen.
And he set out in the name of God and passed through the Gate of Darialan. When he entered Ossetia, Vakhtang was sixteen years old.
Then the kings of Ossetia gathered their troops and brought in forces from Khazaria, and they came to meet him at the river that runs through Darialan and flows down into the plain of Ossetia.
That river is also called the Aragvi, because both rivers rise from the same mountain: the Aragvi of Kartli and the Aragvi of Ossetia.
The two armies camped on either side of the river, for on both banks there were rocky cliffs, with riverside woods and flat ground along the banks.
They kept on guard against each other and held the paths through the cliffs, and they stayed like this for seven days.
During these seven days champions fought single combats at the river. Among the Khazar auxiliaries who were with the Ossetians there was one man, a giant,
named Tarkhan. This Tarkhan the Khazar came out and called in a loud voice, saying:
"I say to you, all you troops of Vakhtang: whoever is the strongest among you, let him come out and fight me."
Among the Persian auxiliary troops that King Vakhtang had, there was one man named Parsman-Parukh.
No one had been able to stand against him in battle, for he had caught many lions with his bare hands.
He went out to fight Tarkhan. Both of them gave a shout and charged at each other.
At the very first clash, Tarkhan brought his sword down on Parsman-Parukh's helmet and split his head down to the shoulders.
Then Vakhtang and his troops were grieved, for there was no one left among them like Parsman-Parukh.
All the troops were terrified and filled with sorrow. Night fell on that day, and Vakhtang went into his tent.
He stood in prayer and begged God with tears, and he did not sit down from his prayer until dawn, asking God for help.
Trusting in God, he resolved to fight Tarkhan himself, for he was as fearless as a bodiless being, and he put his hope in God and in his own strength.
When dawn came, Tarkhan again came down to the riverbank, taunted them again and sought [?] (literally "threat"), and no one could be found among Vakhtang's troops to fight him.
Then Vakhtang said to his troops: "I do not trust in my own strength or in my own courage,
but trusting in God without beginning, the Trinity of one essence, the Creator of all, I will go out myself to fight Tarkhan."

Then the nobles were astonished. They tried to hold Vakhtang back and argued with him in many ways to keep him from the fight, because Vakhtang was a youth and they did not know how he would prove himself.
Vakhtang did not listen to them, but held firm to his decision to fight. He got down from his horse, fell to the ground, and worshipped God. He raised up his hands and said:
"O Lord, Creator of all and Giver of good things in abundance, who exalts those who trust in you!
Be my helper. Send your angel to strengthen me, strike down that lawless man, and put to shame those who blaspheme you, for I do not trust in my own strength but in your mercy."
Vakhtang turned back, mounted his steed, and said to his troops: "Pray to God and do not be afraid."
Vakhtang went forward, and his troops stood behind him. They trembled, and, filled with anxiety, each prayed to God according to his own faith.
1. Here is the fight between Vakhtang and Tarkhan, and the killing of Tarkhan by Vakhtang. Then Vakhtang rode down the slope and took his stand on the bank of the river. He held a lance in his hand.
Tarkhan looked at him and said: "I am one who fights proven giants and heroes, not striplings. Still, I will lower myself to fight even you."

They shouted and charged at each other. At the very first clash Vakhtang struck him with his lance at the belt. The strength of his armor did not protect him: the lance went through and out his back, and killed him.
The Georgians were heartened and filled with joy. They raised a tremendous shout and offered thanks to God.
And Vakhtang got down from his horse on that very spot, fell on the ground, worshipped God and said:
"Blessed are you, O Lord, who sent your angel and struck down my enemy; you are the one who raises up those who trust in you; you are the one who restored
the poor from the earth and lifts up the fallen from the dunghill." He cut off Tarkhan's head, mounted, and went back to his army.
All the troops praised Vakhtang with loud voices and gave thanks to God.
2. Here is the fight between Vakhtang and Bakatar the Ossetian, and the killing of Bakatar by Vakhtang. On the next day another champion came out from among the Ossetians, whose name was Bakatar.
He was a giant. From the time he began to serve as a warrior, no one had been able to stand against him in battle.
He had slain everyone who fought him, for his bow was twelve spans long and his arrow six spans.
This Bakatar came up to the bank of the river, called out in a loud voice, and said:
"King Vakhtang, do not grow proud because you killed Tarkhan. He was not one of the giants, and that is why he was killed by a stripling.
Now, if you yourself come out to fight me, you will meet fierce blows from me, and you will not escape them.
If not, then whoever of your troops comes out, I am ready for him too." Then Vakhtang answered Bakatar and said:
"It was not by my own strength that I defeated Tarkhan, but by the strength of my Creator.
I am no more afraid of you than of a single dog, for the power of Christ is with me, and his precious Cross is my armor."
And Vakhtang drew up his troops and set them in readiness; and he mounted a steed protected by armour, and took up his shield of tiger skin,
which no sword could cut, and he went along the side [?] and took his stand near the river. He called out to Bakatar and said:
"I will not cross the river, because I am a king; I will not go near the army of Ossetia, because if I perish, all my army will perish.
But you are a slave, and if you perish, the armies
of Ossetia, as of a single dog. Cross the river to my side." Then Bakatar the Ossete did as he said and said:
"I, your slayer, will cross the river; but move back three utevani (a measure of distance) from the river's edge."
Then Vakhtang drew back. Baqatar crossed the river and began to shoot arrows.
Then Vakhtang, by the quickness of his eyes, the sharpness of his mind, and the agility of his steed, avoided the arrows:
for he would see the arrow coming from far off, and he would dodge it and nimbly draw closer. On this side and on that, from the armies, came the sounding of trumpets and kettledrums.
And both armies, the Georgians and the Ossetians, shouted with raised voices, so that the mountains and hills shook.
And Baqatar struck Vakhtang's shield with no more than two arrows, and could not pierce it at all.
And then he struck Vakhtang's horse with another arrow and drove it deep into it.
And before Vakhtang's horse fell, he reached Baqatar and brought his sword down on Baqatar's shoulder, and cut him down as far as the heart.
Only then did Vakhtang's horse fall; swiftly he stretched out his hand and seized Baqatar's horse.
And first he fell upon the ground and worshipped God, and offered thanks even more than before.
He mounted Baqatar's horse, came near to his own troops, and said with a loud voice: "Be brave and be strong, for God is on our side."
And those troops advanced in readiness: the men on armored horses and those in mail and helmets in front, behind them the infantry, and behind the infantry the multitude
of horsemen; and thus they advanced against the Ossetians. But the Ossetians took their stand upon the cliff and poured down arrows like heavy rain.
Then King Vakhtang went around behind his army with chosen horsemen, shouting to his troops, strengthening them, and encouraging them.

Then the men on armored horses in front climbed the path up the cliff and came up onto the level ground, and the infantry behind them came up after them, and after them the multitude of horsemen. And there was a mighty battle between them.
And if Vakhtang fought on the right side, the left side trembled; and if he fought on the left side, the right side trembled.
And amid so great a multitude of troops the voice of Vakhtang could be recognized, like the voice of a lion; and two horsemen accompanied him:
Artavaz, his foster-brother, son of Saurmag the commander-in-chief (spaspet), and Bivritian the royal prince. And they too fought bravely. Then the Ossetians were defeated, and their camp fled.

They were shot down and taken captive; but most of the fleeing Ossetians were seized alive in order to ransom back the captives, the Georgians who had earlier been carried off as captives by the Ossetians.
When they returned from the pursuit, they encamped in their own camp; they rested three days and offered thanks to God.
And then they spread out to plunder Ossetia. They destroyed their cities and took countless captives and spoils.
And he subjugated the Ossetians and the Kipchaks, and he built the Gates of Ossetia, which we call Darial.
And on it he built high towers, and he set the nearby mountaineers there as guards.
The great peoples of the Ossetians and the Kipchaks are not able to come out without the command of the king of the Georgians.

And they went out to the land of the Pechenegs, for at that time the land of the Pechenegs lay there, bordering Ossetia, beyond the river of Ossetia, and the land of the Jiks was also there. After many
times had passed, the Pechenegs and the Jiks were driven out by the Turks. The Pechenegs went off toward the west, and the Jiks settled at the far end of Abkhazia.
And Vakhtang plundered the land of the Pechenegs and the land of the Jiks, and he turned back and came again to Ossetia.
And the kings of the Ossetians had fled to the fortresses of the Caucasus. Envoys went back and forth between them, and they made peace.
And in exchange for his sister, the Ossetians asked Vakhtang for thirty thousand captives of Ossetia, all of them the best, whom the Ossetians named one by one.
And Vakhtang gave thirty thousand captives for his sister, and he brought her back.
And all the Georgian captives that the Ossetians had taken during those six years, he ransomed them all back, one for one,
and he took hostages from the Ossetians, and for the hostages he gave another thirty thousand captives. And the captives of Kartli whom he ransomed back numbered three hundred and fifty thousand,
and the Ossetian captives who remained besides those exchanged numbered, by count, six hundred and fifty thousand, not counting the Pechenegs and the Jiks.
And all this was accomplished in four months. Then the king dismissed the Persian nobles and the kings of the Caucasians with great gifts,
and he sent his sister Mirandukht and all the captives by the road of Darial, while he himself, with the great army of Kartli, set out by the road of Abkhazia.
Patiently and fearlessly he began to make war on the fortresses of Abkhazia.
For the king of the Greeks, Leo the Great, was occupied with the war against the Persians and was unable to send troops to Abkhazia;
and in three years he captured all the fortresses of Abkhazia as far as Tsikhegoji. And he came to his home, to the royal city of Mtskheta.
His mother and his sisters came out to meet him, and the multitude of the city, men and women, spread
their kerchiefs and their garments under his feet.
And they showered drachmas and darics on his head, and with raised voices they sang his praises, for no king had ever waged so mighty a campaign.
Then King Vakhtang offered thanks to God with many prayers and all-night vigils, and with gifts to the poor.
And he gave gifts to his people, and he raised to noble rank the horsemen, the servants who had been brave and had proved themselves in that war with the Ossetians.
And from the spoils he sent gifts to his mother's brother, Varaz-Bakur: a thousand slaves, a thousand riding horses, and a thousand geldings.
And he also sent to the king of the Persians ten thousand slaves, ten thousand riding horses, and ten thousand geldings.
He sent all this to the king of the Persians by the hand of Bishop Binkaran, and he asked the king of the Persians for his daughter in marriage.
And the king of the Persians gave him his daughter as a wife. Her name was Balendukht.
He also gave him Armenia and all the kings of the Caucasus as a dowry. With her he sent a letter, and on its patrutsag [?] was written:
"From Hormizd, king of all kings, to Vakhtang, Varan-Khusro-Tang, valiant king of ten kings."
In it he told him about the war with the Caesar, because the Caesar had set out to make war on the Persians.
Then Vakhtang informed all his troops and all the kings of the Caucasus. They gathered and camped on both sides of the Mtkvari, about two hundred thousand of them. Then he was joined by
Varaz-Bakur, his mother's brother and the eristavi of Ran, who came by order of the king of the Persians with the troops of Adarbadagan, Ran and Movakan, about two hundred thousand horsemen.
At that time Vakhtang was twenty-two years old. He was taller than anyone else of his time, the most beautiful in appearance, and mighty in strength.

Wearing armour and on foot, he would catch up with a deer, grab it by the horn and hold it fast. He would lift an armoured horse onto his shoulders and carry it up from Mtskheta to the fortress of Armazi.
He was his father's only son. One of his sisters, Khuarandze, was also strong and beautiful.
Of the line of the believing King Mirian, only Vakhtang and his sisters remained. They were descendants of Bakar, son of Mirian.
Mirian and Gregory, however, were of the line of Rev, who was also a son of Mirian. They held Kukheti and lived in the fortress-city of Rustavi.
For the family had dwindled because its members killed one another. From King Mirian to King Vakhtang, eight generations and ten kings had passed away,
and one hundred and fifty-seven years. Eight bishops who held the true faith had passed away, and the others were corrupters of the faith.
Here: Vakhtang Gorgasali goes to Greece to make war. Vakhtang set out to invade Greece.
They reached Armenia, and at Peroz-Kapa, where the Peroz mentioned earlier had once built a fortress, the eristavis of Armenia joined them:
Arev of Siunik, Juansher of Vaspurakan, Amazasp of Taron from the city built by Gregory, and Trdat of the line of the great Trdat.
They besieged the fortress-city called Karakhpola, which is now called the city of Karnu. And
they fought against it, but they could not take it, because it had three high walls.
They left two eristavis with twelve thousand horsemen to fight against the city.
Vakhtang went on to Pontus and on the way laid waste to three cities: Anzoreti, Ekletsi and Steri. Then the armies besieged the great city of Pontus on the seashore.
They fought for three months, and the army reached as far as the city of Constantine. Whenever the Persians found servants of the church, they killed them.
But King Vakhtang ordered the troops of Armenia and all the Persians not to kill any monastics, but to take them captive. He said to them:
"When my father's father Mirian went with the king of the Persians, his nephew, to make war on the Greeks,
they did things like this to monastics and servants of the church, and their countless troops were defeated in a terrible defeat by small armies.
From that time the Greeks received this boundary from us Georgians, to the east of this sea.
The seat of the first kings was at Andzianjor, where the tomb of the great teacher Gregory now is, and from there our kings were driven out.
We have come down a ten days' journey and have turned to the north.
And we too hold the faith of the Greeks and confess Christ, who is the true God of all.

"Or have you not heard of the miracles that were worked in the time of King Constantine, when the Cross was carried before him? Or of the miracles that were worked in the land of the Greeks in the time of Julian, the idolatrous king?
How an arrow from heaven killed him, and the armies of the Greeks gathered and made Jovian king;
but he would not accept it until they had smashed the idols and set up crosses. And they placed upon him the crown
of the king; but an angel of the Lord took up the crown and set it on the head of Jovian, the true king.
And there was a voice from heaven, which said to Khosrow-Tang, king of the Persians:
"Stop fighting Jovian [?], for by the power of the Cross he cannot be defeated." And from then on the king and Khosrow were friends, until both of them died.
"Or you, the inhabitants of Armenia, the Arsacids, the Bivritian patiakhshes (governors):
do you not remember the deeds of Gregory the Parthian and of his opponent, King Trdat the Arsacid? How he was cast down because of his pride and became a boar?
But Gregory converted him, and from that time he became a laborer for the churches. Trdat built a great church, carrying it on his own back, for he was a giant.
And you, the inhabitants of Kartli, kinsmen of the kings of Kartli, who today have been placed in positions of authority by us,
the kings, who are of the lineage of Nimrod the giant, who appeared on the earth before all other kings;
who by his strength would lead a lion like a young goat, and would catch wild asses and gazelles on foot. For his strength grew so great
that all the peoples descended from Noah submitted to him, until he was able to build a city. He made its stones of gold and its steps of silver,
and he built around it with brick and lime. He made the tops of the doors and windows of jacinth and emerald, so that because of their light the night could not grow dark.
And he built temples and towers in it that are beyond your power to conceive; the wisdom of each one of them is beyond imagining,
the wisdom that had been given to him, until he raised up a structure three days' journey high, which he had made as an ascent of steps upon the walls. And he wished to go up
to heaven and see those who dwell in heaven. But when he had passed the boundary of the air and entered the region of the stars,
the workers could no longer work, for the gold and silver were melting. From there onward lies the domain of the ethereal fire,
which burns fiercely because of the turning of the firmament. And from there he heard the counsel of the seven hosts of heaven, by which people were confounded.
And every man, each with his own kin, came to speak a separate language. They no longer understood the speech of one another, and they went away.
"And to Nimrod he said in the Persian language: 'I am the angel Michael, who has been appointed by God to rule over the east.'
Go out of that city, for God protects that city until Paradise appears, which stands near that building of yours,
in which is this mountain from which the sun rises, and from it come out two rivers: the Nile and the Gihon.
For the Gihon carries fragrant wood and grass out of Paradise, which is mixed with musk. Now go away.
And settle between the two rivers, the Euphrates and the Tigris, and let these peoples go wherever each one wishes, for the Lord has sent them out.
Your kingdom will reign over all kings, but in the last times the King of heaven, whom you wish to see, will come among a despised people;
fear of him will make the pleasures of the world pass away, and kings will give up their kingship and seek poverty.
Then God will see you in torment and will save you." "And they all left the city and went away.
And he left those who spoke Indian in India, the Sindhis in Sind, the Romans in Rome, the Greeks in Greece,
Gog and Magog in the land of Magog, and the Persians in Persia. The first language was Assyrian, and these are the seven languages that were spoken up to the time of Nimrod.
I have told you this because our fathers kept this book hidden, but godly zeal compelled me to speak of it,
since it was through this that our father Mirian received the Gospel of Christ through Nino.
"Did our fathers not receive tribute before the coming of Christ, and have you grown weak since then, now that these Greeks are fighting against us?
And he saw Nimrod in hell and delivered him. He is the first of all kings, and Daniel also bears witness that Michael has been appointed as the power over the Persians.
And you, all Georgians, have seen these miracles that Nino performed. Or do you think that God has abandoned the Greeks?
Did they not crush the greater lands of the Persians and annex them? Today it is the sixth month since they heard the news of our campaign;
the Caesar has turned back because they heard of our invasion, and now he has drawn near to fight us.
Now therefore, all peoples, serve the Lord God and stop harming the churches."
And when he had said all this, he sent out a herald so that all the members of religious orders would come out of their hiding places. He also released the captives to go wherever they wished.

And a multitude of priests and deacons, members of religious orders, monks and encratites came out of caves and down from the mountains, and most of them came from the city of Pontus, for the city had been under siege for only four months.
With them were two men: Peter the priest, one of the disciples of Gregory the Theologian, who served as priest at his tomb, and Samuel the monk.
They came before Vakhtang to thank him for releasing the captives and for freeing the churches and the priests.
And when they had said the prayer, the king was pleased and looked on them with favour, and he ordered that all the captives and the clergy be brought in,
the sick people whom he had released, for all the sick had come out of the city.
To the sick he gave provisions and to the young men three drachmas each, and he let them go. But he kept Peter the priest and Samuel the monk with him.
And when those troops went off to their tents, the king went in to supper. The king said to Peter:
"May this deed of mine have pleased God, for I have spared the churches and released the captives." Peter said:
"Should your servant speak boldly before you, or should I give you false praise?" The king said to him:
"Speak, for I seek nothing but to be corrected, so that we may be freed from falsehood." Peter said:
"Churches of flesh are worth more before God than churches of stone. When a church of stone is destroyed, it is rebuilt with the same stone;
But when churches of flesh are destroyed, no one can heal them, neither a physician nor a king.
Now, how many bodies of righteous men you have struck down! Scripture says this about the blood of Abel: all that blood was washed away by the destruction in Noah's time.

And for the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah (literally "son of Baruch"), he paid the Jews back for every outrage, as Isaiah says: 'Take up and destroy all their offspring.' This was done through Titus and Vespasian.
Or have you not read in the books of Moses how many souls died for that one act of fornication, when an Israelite committed fornication with a woman of foreign race?
Now then, how many virgins, who are temples of God, have been defiled by your soldiers!"
And the king said: "Do you not see how Jovian stayed with the wicked Julian in order to protect the churches?
And if a man stumbles, it is better to fall completely." Peter said to him:
"I do not knock you down when you stumble. Instead, I raise you up when you have fallen, as David was raised from his sin concerning Uriah.
I do not want you to be like a man who builds with his right hand and tears down with his left,
nor like those who bless with their mouths but curse and revile in their hearts,
but like the kings of good memory, who ruled this world and were not cut off from the Kingdom of Heaven:
David, Solomon and Constantine, Jovian, and all who were like them.
But how are you like Jovian? Who is lord over you, holding his sword over your neck, as Julian held his over Jovian's?
Or where have you been harmed, as Jovian was harmed by Julian?
Or whom does God see that he has made lord over you, who would have to answer before God for your righteousness?
Did he not make you lord over all these people, and place them all under you?
From now on God will demand from your hands every evil deed, and he will pay you back for it, unless you repent."
The king said to him: "I want to justify myself, but you have judged my wrongdoing rightly."
Peter said to him: "Since you have given way to confession, your sin has been taken away from you.
But now I will tell you what is in your heart. It was not ignorance that moved you to make war on the sons of God, but your wish to help your kinsmen, the Persians.
Do you not know that the Greeks are God's kin because of the promise, when he called them children of God and gave them the seal with which he shattered hell, and that seal is the Cross?"
The king said: "Now what do you want?" Peter said to him:
"I want you to put out this fire that you yourself lit, and to be a friend of the Caesar, as you have been a friend of the Persians until today."
The king answered: "This is what I want: that through your prayer this night you show me the Emperor and me brought together,
and how there may be love between us, and I will know that this intention of yours toward me is pleasing to Christ."
Peter said: "This request of yours weighs heavily on me, for this belongs to chosen men, who are like angels in their perfect deeds,
and they live among these rocks, and such a thing as you ask is possible for them to do.
Give me time, so that I may go and entreat them and tell them your command, and through their prayer your intention will be fulfilled;
but we hold ourselves in contempt, for we are sinful men; may God not see it as presumption."
The monk Samuel rebuked him and said: "Priest, you think of the work of God as though it were the work of men.
Or have you not read how God says to Polycarp: 'If the angels did not stumble at the virtue of men, I would be crucified in every city, so that I might save all'?
Or is Ahab, king of Israel, greater than the king of the Christians? Isaiah says to him, 'Ask for a sign in the height or in the depth,' and for his sake said, 'A virgin shall conceive.'
Or who was it who said to the Israelite, 'Whatever you ask in my name will be given to you'? Joshua said to the firmament of heaven, 'Turn back,' and it turned back three degrees.
Now the word of your humility is good, Peter, but it is a stumbling block to men of little faith.
But you, O king, help us a little with your faith, for the prayer of this afflicted city will accomplish your will." And the holy men went to their dwelling.
The king prayed for a long time and lay down, and in his sleep, behold, the woman came, who was Saint Nino, and said:

"Arise, O king, and go carefully to meet them, for two kings, of heaven and of earth, are coming to you." And it seemed that he looked, and first he saw the image of a woman [?], like that of Constantine;
and he hurried there and saw two thrones: on one sat a youth in armour, wearing a crown;
and on the second throne he saw an old man sitting, wrapped in a white cloth, and on his head lay a crown of light, not of gold, and Nino sat at his feet;
And Peter the priest held Vakhtang's right hand, and Samuel the monk held his left. And Samuel said:
"First fall down before that great prince of heaven, Gregory." He went and bowed down. And Gregory said:
"What is this evil you have done, man? You have laid waste my camp and given my flocks to the beasts to eat.
Were it not for these two who stand beside you, and for the sake of the virtue of this woman, who labours constantly with Mary on your behalf,
I would have taken vengeance on you, as on your fathers, who put their hope in consuming fire and not in the radiance that gives light to all."
And he gave him his hand and kissed him. Then, as it seemed, he reached out his hand to a crown of light, and, as it seemed, he gave a crown like it to Vakhtang and said:
"Put that on Peter." And Peter took from that same crown something that seemed lesser and put it on Samuel the monk. And Nino said to Vakhtang:
"Now then, go to the king and receive your gift." He went to the king, and they kissed each other. The king made room for him on his throne and seated him beside himself.
And he gave him a ring from his hand, whose stone was exceedingly bright, and the emperor said:
"If you wish me to give you a crown, promise the one who stands above us that you will fight against his enemies
and receive the crown from him." Vakhtang looked around and saw a cross that had a crown on its arms,
and the sight of the cross filled him with trembling even more, for the awe it caused was more terrible, and he fell silent.
Then Nino rose and looked toward Peter and Samuel, and with one voice they said:
"We stand surety that he will prosper more than all, O invincible Cross."
The emperor stretched out his hand, took the crown from the cross, and placed it on Vakhtang's head.
As they began to go out, the bishop called out three times and said: "Vakhtang, Vakhtang, Vakhtang!
"You were more faithful than all others among the race of the Persians." Second:
"Through you churches were built and bishops were appointed, along with a chief of bishops." And third:

"He also received the crown of martyrdom." And he came out. Then, as it seemed, he called Peter and Samuel while he was still asleep, and told them the vision while still asleep, and they interpreted it:
"The one you saw on the thrones, crowned with light, is the great teacher Gregory. When he gave me something from his crown, he gave me the primacy over the bishops.
When I gave something from my crown to my companion, it means he is to be made bishop by me. The one you saw adorned with crowns of gold is the emperor.
When he gave you a ring, it means you will be given a daughter of his as your wife, and all the territory of Kartli that he took will be given back to you.
When he gave you the crown from the cross, it means you will come through great struggles with the help of the cross.
When our teacher called you three times, he was asking God for three gifts for you:
that through you the truth be confirmed by the catholicoses and bishops of Kartli, and that you overcome your enemies until the day of your death.
And at your death you will receive the crown of martyrdom in battle; you will not fall into the hands of your enemies.
All this will be fulfilled until you grow weak and old."
When King Vakhtang woke up, he thanked God, who had revealed everything to him. He quickly summoned Peter and Samuel and said to them: "What did you see?"
They answered: "You tell us, O king. We stood one on your right and one on your left while you stood before those seated on the thrones, the emperor and the Theologian.
And then our same queen calmed the teacher who was angry with you, and placed you in his hands." The king said to them:
"Be silent, holy men, for you have seen everything together with me. Now, what do you want done about this city, which is on the point of being destroyed?
Or what are we to do with these captives in our hands, who number more than ten thousand?
Now news has quickly gone out from here that the king of the Persians has set out for the land of Jazira,
and that he has passed through Philistia in pursuit of the emperor, who devastated the land of the Persians while the Persian king was unable to fight him.
But when the emperor learned that we had come into their land, he hurried to fight against us. And we see that the king of the Persians is coming against us in force.
We know that the Persian armies are larger than the armies of Armenia and Kartli, and there is no true believer among us.
As for those whom our father Mirian planted in the faith, or Trdat, my kinsman on my mother's side, we know the faith of all of them here: it is full of error.
"Otherwise, when what I have done comes out, this maternal uncle of mine may grow angry, and we will fight each other and become a laughing-stock to all our enemies.
So let me do this: when our troops arrive and tell us the emperor is coming, we will withdraw at that point.
Let us first tell him about this matter when the emperor comes and draws near to us. Then we will do whatever your holiness advises, and not a single one of his captives will be missing."
Peter went to the emperor, and Samuel stood before the king. The next day a [?] came and reported to the king
that the troops of the Greeks had entered Constantinople. King Vakhtang summoned his maternal uncle and all the kings and said:
"What do you say? You know how many troops the Greeks have, how cunning they are in battle, and how skilled they are at sea with ships.
These are the very men who invaded Persia, the land of heroes and giants, and the Persians could not stand against them in battle.
Now I am afraid that their troops may come by ship, cut off our road, and slaughter us as if we were penned in a sheepfold.
So let us move from here and camp on the southern side of the sea, so that we have a road open to us in bad times and in good."
The army broke camp from around the city and marched five days' journey to the south, and they halted on the side toward Speri. The people of the city, who had been brought close to death, came out
and thanked Vakhtang. They gave him a gift of a thousand litrai of gold and five hundred pieces of brocade, and the people went out in peace to trade and get provisions.
When Peter came before the king, the emperor, he told him everything.
The emperor rejoiced greatly, and he granted Vakhtang his wish in everything he had seen in the vision.
He sent Peter the priest back, and sent word with a promise and a mighty oath that Vakhtang would be his equal in kingship. But both of them [?]
[?] the Persian troops who were with Vakhtang should be struck down, [?] so that they would not go up from their domains, when Vakhtang and he met. And while Peter and
the envoys were on their way to Vakhtang, the emperor entered Constantinople and sent out five hundred dromons, with five hundred men sitting in each,
and he ordered them to approach Vakhtang and hold their position without fighting. The emperor himself set out along the road of Pontus with eight hundred thousand men.
When those naval forces drew near, the Persians wanted to fight them, but the king held them back and did not let them go into battle.
When the Caesar's envoy and Peter presented the gifts, the envoy had a secret message and also a public message. And he said openly:
"Do not flee. Stay until I come, so that we may also slaughter the Persians who are with you, those who were left to you alive when we invaded Persia."
But in secret they brought him a cross and a crown as a pledge of mediation, along with a garment for his body, and he said:
"When we meet, I will give you the fortress of Tukhari and the borders of Kartli." King Vakhtang gave his answer publicly, saying:
"We have come here for no other reason than to fight you. Now come here, and if you do not, we will come to Constantinople." And in secret he sent him a message, saying:
"Do not urge another to do what does not befit your love of God and what you would not do yourself, for treachery is not the way of honorable men.
Even if I now hand the Persians over to you, would my name not be made false? And many of them hold the love of Christ more than we do,
but out of fear of them they cannot make it known. Now give the command that we carry out this affair of ours in peace, as [?] Ivbimianos and all the Persians [?].
And after this, when our affair is settled, I will gather them into your hand on better terms. Let no shameful deed be done,
and let no act of disorder be done by you, so that your people do not fall by the edge of the sword. For your people have grown arrogant
over their victory over the Persians. But the Persians are not frightened at all; rather, in their rivalry with you they are eager for battle:
either they would die, or they would avenge their blood. But if these troops of yours fight beyond this point, I am to be held innocent."
And with him went as envoys Varaz-Mihr, the brother of his foster-father, and Samuel the monk.

Now the emperor had arrived at the city of Pontus, and the people of Pontus had come out to meet him. They offered praise and thanks to King Vakhtang, because he had spared them and had not given them over to death.
When King Vakhtang's envoys reached the city, they presented gifts: a thousand mithqals of musk, five hundred [measures] of ambergris, and a thousand litrai of aloe-wood.
And a band of King Vakhtang's had gone out to plunder. The Greek [?] (mkvirtskhlni) attacked them, and with them horsemen gathered from the valleys and cities, about three hundred thousand.
But King Vakhtang was holding the troops back from going to [the aid of] those plunderers [?], until his mother's brother, the eristavi of the Persians, came and said to Vakhtang in anger:
"O serpent and offspring of an asp! Do you not know that your father's mother was a Greek, a relative of Ivbimianos?
The nature of your father's mother has overcome you. You have taken hold of the love of that crucified dead man, and you want to hand us over into the hands of the Greeks." But Vakhtang said:
"There you are: you and the Greeks! And you will see the power of that man who died, and of that living one, your hope [?]."
And they sounded the trumpet, and all Armenia, the Persians and the king of Derbent went out. But King
Vakhtang and the Georgians went out to watch and took their stand. The king mounted a white elephant. They were drawn up on the sea-shore, which is a meadow, the gravel bank of Khertvisi.
Before the Persian army arrived, the Greeks had killed twenty-seven thousand of those people. The battle grew fierce, and they killed Vakhtang's mother's brother,
the eristavi of the Persians. They also killed Ipajaj, king of the Lekians, and many chief princes, and the camp of the East was defeated.
The Greek commander was Palekarpos of Loghoti, the king's sister's son, and he was mighty. He had killed the strong warriors of the Persians, and it was he who also killed this eristavi.
Then King Vakhtang got down from the chariot and said: "Not what we wanted, but what pleased God [has come to pass],
for we spoke of peace, but the arrogance of the Persians insulted God, and God took vengeance, and they killed the eristavi of Ran.
For this all Persia mourns, as if for the devastation of Persia. Now the arrogance of the Persians has been brought low. Bring the cross and let us carry it before us,
so that they may be defeated by the very thing by which they defeated us. Be sons of strength. Let none of you fight against one another through another [?], and do not seek victory over the enemies;
but let your hands be like my hands, so that we may not be utterly defeated.
Not only shall we pursue them here, but as far as Adarbadagan, as ravens are chased by their own young hawks [?]."
And Peter the priest brought the cross, and the king said to him: "Stand before the face of the enemy and of our people, and say to everyone: 'Bow down to the cross, and
we shall defeat the enemy'; and whoever does not bow down, kill him." And he ordered Demetre, his eristavi, and Juansher the spaspet to go along with the cross.
And the herald cried out loudly: "Whoever does not bow down to the cross shall be put to death." And all the people came, bowed down, and stood before the cross.
But Borzo, the king of Movakan, said: "I will not abandon the burning light, and I will not bow down to [?] wood
that is adorned with gold and carbuncles." And Juansher the spaspet struck him with a lance, and his carcass fell.
From then on no one dared to blaspheme the cross any more, and the people made a vow to King Vakhtang, saying:
"If the cross helps us, we shall have no other god except the Crucified One."
And the king dismounted and bowed down to it, and all the people with him, and the king said:
"Show your power to this unbelieving people of yours, so that you may bring them to faith, O Lord God, your believers;
though they die, yet they are alive, and your living ones are strong through you, the Living One." And the Greek troops came out like lightning.
But Polycarp, like a wolf smeared with blood and like an enraged lion, shouted out and insulted those troops. And the king said:
"Who among you is a man who will fight him and be worthy of my kingship?" The herald went around twice, and no one dared to say a word.
Here: the combat of Vakhtang Gorgasali and Polycarp, the commander of the Greeks, and the killing of Polycarp by Vakhtang. Then Vakhtang said:
"A man is not made strong by strength, but God gives strength. And I trust in your strength, and like David I go out with the sign
of the cross; give me strength as you gave David against Goliath, for this man too has come against your cross with reproach and contempt;
when he saw the cross raised up as a strength for us, he did not flee from it, but in hope of its strength they went out to battle." And he said:
"You saw the proud, O God, and humbled him; again you saw the afflicted and delivered him.
As for that man, I hold him in contempt and do not fear him, for the strength given by you is great, and by it I shall prevail;
but I fear you, for you hear the voices of the humble, and I call on you as my helper."
He drew his sword and touched it to the cross, and went out between the battle lines, and said:
"A lion does not fight an ox, for I am a king and you are a slave; but I lay down my life for this people in humility, so that they may believe in the power of the cross."
And Polycarp charged at him. But Vakhtang approached quietly and slowly.
And both battle lines shouted with a terrible cry, and that cry was like the sound of thunder, and the earth shook with it.
And Polycarp struck Vakhtang's shield, which was made of tiger skin, with his lance, and drove it about one cubit through the shield, for the lance was as thick as a man's arm.
And the king let the shield go with his lance in it, and charged him face to face, and struck him with his sword on the helmet, and split his head down to the shoulders.
And he reached out his hand, grasped half of his head, brought it before the Cross, and said:
"Let this be the share of everyone who turns away from you." And Vakhtang's troops charged the Greek troops and routed them, and
cut them down band by band, and pinned them against the seashore. None of them escaped, except those who managed to reach the sea and fled by ship.
On that day forty-three thousand of Vakhtang's troops were killed, and seventy-two thousand of the Greek troops were killed. And one hundred and twenty-five thousand of them were taken captive.
And when Vakhtang's troops returned and came to the body of Varaz-Bakur, Vakhtang's maternal uncle, they mourned him, and embalmed him with aloes and myrrh, and sent him to Barda.
But King Vakhtang summoned all the troops, and ordered that all the captives be brought, and they brought them with none missing.
And all of them together, men and women, numbered seven hundred and eighty thousand.
And he sent all of them to the emperor in the care of Nasre and Adarnase, his eristavs.
And he wrote a letter that said: "The wisdom of God is beyond understanding, and the will of God overcomes the wisdom and will of men.
I know that this deed done by Polycarp was not your will, nor was it my will,
what my maternal uncle did; and both of these evildoers were caught by their own evil.
God did this so that these new plantings might be brought to faith through fear of him, just as he made a cause for rejoicing over the prodigal son.
But you are the firstborn sons of God, and you are always his. Now I have been comforted for this grief over my maternal uncle, your sister's son,
when I took vengeance on his killers. And you, be comforted for this people, seven hundred and eighty thousand of whom God has rescued.
And if you order a meeting with me, make haste; and if not, then through an envoy
settle our affairs. For staying here has become hard for us because this land has been laid waste." Until the envoys arrived, the emperor was very grieved.

But when they told him that all the captives, both those taken earlier and those taken from the routed army, had been released with none missing, he rejoiced greatly, and everyone put aside their grief.

And the emperor boarded a ship and set out with three hundred dromons. He came lightly equipped to the seashore and summoned Vakhtang. They made a covenant and swore oaths to each other, and settled the matter of pledges.
And the emperor gave back the border region of Kartli: the fortress of Tukhari and all of Klarjeti, from the sea as far as Arsiani, and the valleys that reach to Ghado.
And the emperor asked for the border region of Greece, the land along the seacoast, which is Abkhazeti, and spoke as follows:
"From the Egris River as far as the river of Little Khazaria, this has been the border of Greece since the time of Alexander, and you have now taken it from us by force.
Now give it back to us, and when you take away your wife, my daughter,
"Then I will give you land from it." And he wrote over to him the land between the Egris-tsqali and Klisura as a dowry, and Vakhtang gave the rest of Abkhazia back to the Greeks.
And Vakhtang came back by way of Klarjeti, and he dismissed his troops by way of Somkhiti (Armenia).
And when he reached Tukhari, he looked at the fortress and liked it, and he said:
"Truly you are a fortress!" And as he went on, he saw a rock in the middle of Klarjeti, at a village called Artanuji.
And he summoned Artavaz, his foster-brother, and appointed him eristavi (duke), and ordered him to build the fortress of Artanuji.
And he ordered him to find a place in that gorge suitable for a monastery and to build a church, and
they made it into a monastery, like the monasteries they had seen in Greece. And he said to Artavaz:
"If the Persians grow stronger than us, our refuge is to be here."
And Artavaz built the fortress of Artanuji, and the monastery that is Opiza, and three churches:
in the villages of Meria, Shindoba and Akhiza. And he restored the fortress of Akhiza and made it a cave-stronghold.
And when Vakhtang came on and arrived at his own city, Mtskheta, there was great joy and thanksgiving to God, because he had come in peace.
And he gave great gifts to his people. But when the king of the Persians learned that Vakhtang had gone over to the side of the Greeks, he turned back to Persia and died.
And his son sat as king, and three years passed while he was coming of age.
And his wife bore King Vakhtang twins, a son and a daughter, and Queen Balendukht, daughter of the king of the Persians, died in childbirth.
And Vakhtang named his son Darchil in Persian and Dachi in Georgian.

At that time King Vakhtang had no chance to bring home his wife, the daughter of the king of the Greeks, nor to bring the catholicos and the bishops, because he was waiting for the king of the Persians to come.
He was strengthening the fortresses and cities, equipping the horsemen, and preparing for war with the Persians.
Then he threw Binkaran the deceiver, the bishop of the fire-worshippers, into prison, and he slaughtered and drove out all the fire-worshippers from the borders of Kartli.
And after three years the king of the Persians set out to make war on Vakhtang. He reached Indabriani [?] and camped there. And Vakhtang sent
to the king of the Greeks and sent him word: "Behold, this is the day I promised you, when I would shut the Persians up in your hand.
See, I have drawn them into the middle of the borders of Kartli, all their men, about three hundred thousand."
For he [the Persian king] had expected to increase his army from Armenia and from the kings of the Caucasians, but they did not dare to join him.
For some of them had hope in the Crucified One; but those who had been overcome by the devil, the kings of Darubandi (Derbent), joined him.
"Now I have fulfilled the promise I made: wherever I found a fire-temple, I filled it with dung,
and I have handed over their magi and their seers to cruel torture, and I put the deceiver Binkaran in prison, and he escaped death."
He then brought the Persians to Kartli, and I installed Michael, a faithful man, as bishop. But Binkaran died when he reached the borders of Kartli.
Now let your troops hurry here, so that all the enemies of the Cross may fall here, and you will be rid of all your enemies.
But if he defeats us, he will grow strong and will enter your borders by the road of Shimshati."
But before King Vakhtang's envoys arrived, the emperor had gone off toward the land of Khazaria, so he was not free to come to Kartli.
Then Vakhtang strengthened the fortresses of the city. He kept with him the best fighters of his people, about one hundred thousand horsemen and one hundred thousand foot soldiers,
and he camped them from Dighomi as far as the Gate of Kartli, and the Persians camped from Tskhenis-Terpi downward.
Here is the coming of the Persians to Kartli to make war on Vakhtang Gorgasali. Vakhtang widened the bridge of Mogvta to about sixty arm-lengths, so that the troops could move across it.

The king and Juansher the spaspet (commander-in-chief) stationed themselves at Mtskheta. He left Nasra and Mirdat in command of the troops of Somkhiti and Kartli, who were stationed on the Armazi side.
Whenever the Persians attacked on the Armazi side, they would come out from Mtskheta to fight. Whenever that army crossed from Mtskheta to the other side, they would join battle on the Aragvi.
Sometimes they would cross the ford of the Mtkvari and fight at the ford of Tbilisi. On some days the one side won, and on other days the other.
King Vakhtang had a golden helmet made, with a wolf depicted on the front and a lion on the back.
Wherever the Georgians were being beaten, he would go there and slaughter the Persian army as a lion slaughters wild asses.
From then on the Persians could no longer stand against him in battle, because they had learned to recognize the one whose helmet bore a wolf and a lion. Whenever they saw Vakhtang, they would say:
"Dur az gorgasal," which means, "Keep away from the wolf's head." From this King Vakhtang was given the name Gorgasali.
The fighting between them went on for only four months. Then an envoy came from the emperor and brought gifts to Vakhtang.
He also brought eighty thousand horsemen from the Greek troops, and the emperor wrote to Vakhtang as follows:
"I have become engaged in war with the Khagan. I have sent you eighty thousand horsemen, and I have written to Leo:
'If you need an army, it is at your disposal from Melitene as far as Lamed, and on this side as far as the city of Karnu.' And I have ordered Leo to be at your service."
The Greek army had arrived in Javakheti. When the king of the Persians learned that the Greeks had come to help them, he began to negotiate with Vakhtang.
He sent word through his envoy, saying: "Why should we destroy one another? We are kinsmen, sons of Nimrod.
If fire is God, then let it defend itself. But let us hold to the friendship of our fathers.
Let each of us serve whatever pleases his own soul."
When the envoy came and told King Vakhtang the whole proposal of the Persian king, it pleased Vakhtang and all his people.
And King Vakhtang gave gifts, sent his envoy to him, and said:
"You have seen the power of the Cross, for all kings used to bring us tribute until the appearance of the Crucified One.
Since he appeared, all who worship him have defeated you in his presence. Your tributaries, the Greeks, are fighting you on this side, and they have destroyed the places where fire is worshipped.
Now, if you fight us because we will not abandon our faith, let us die for him, as he died for us, and he will raise us up.
But if you keep your word, and fire is not made our god by you, and Christ is our God, I will call you father and lord.
Although we are the firstborn, still you shall sit on the thrones of our father."
When they told him Vakhtang's words, he accepted them and sent a great gift to Gorgasali, and with it a crown set with carbuncles, and they fixed a time for a meeting.
The king of the Persians set out and camped at Rustavi. At dawn they came out and took up position on the plain of Kalai, because the town of Tbilisi and Kalai too were lying in ruins at that time.
King Vakhtang camped at Jachu, and both kings met on that same plain and greeted
each other, and each made an inviolable covenant on his own faith.
On that day Gorgasali invited the king of the Persians, together with his army, to Tbilisi. Gorgasali presented him with a thousand female servants, five hundred male slaves,
five hundred brocade skaramangi robes, five hundred bizioni zuzma [?], ten thousand [?] (ḳhdali) horses, five hundred pack horses, three hundred mules, four thousand cattle,
and ten thousand sheep. On the third day Gorgasali went to him and took with him Leo, the emperor's proconsul, and they held a council.
The proconsul urged Gorgasali to make peace between the emperor and Khosrow,
because the Greeks were afraid that the Persians might invade Greece and lay it waste, since all the armies of Greece were in Khazaria.
Khosrow said to Gorgasali: "Ask of me whatever you wish, for yourself or for anyone else you wish."
And Gorgasali said: "I wish that it may be so. Peace be between you and Caesar." Khosrow said:
"Your request weighs heavily on me, for when the Greeks find an opportunity against us, they show no mercy."
I made this friendship with you so that I might go into Greece and take vengeance on them. And look:
this is the tenth day since the envoy of the king of the Khazars arrived, and you do not know the cause of our enmity.
But now I will tell you of their insolence toward us, and then I will do your will, since I promised you with a mighty oath that I would do nothing against your will." And he said:
"You know that our border lies on this side of the sea, divided off since the time of Noah. Now he is fighting me in Jazira and Sham, and the cities are laid waste, and Sham is our kingdom.
Half of Jazira, as our fathers ordained, is your portion, and the Greeks have taken it,
and I was going in for this very purpose, to take it back. Now as for the part that belongs to your fathers, divide it yourself; that is between you and the Greeks.
But let the Greeks give me the rest of Jazira; that is what I have asked of you."
When Leo the proconsul heard this, he rejoiced greatly, bowed down to both kings, and said:
"Let the five cities of Jazira be yours, on your side, for we give back to you the half of Sicily which we took from you. And in our days let there be peace between you and him."
And the king said: "Who knows whether the king of the Greeks will be content with what we have done?" And Leo said:
"When he sent me forth against the might of this king, a certain monk with knowledge of God told our king that peace among all three of these kings is pleasing to God.
And so it came to pass. And Caesar commanded a scribe, and he wrote a letter of peace.
And behold, his letter is written here." As he said this, they read the letter. It was written with an oath:

"Apart from what the king of the Persians gave to Jovian, I will claim nothing from you." And the king of the Persians summoned the envoy of the king of the Khazars, and told him of the Persians' rising against the Greeks.
Then the king of the Persians took paper and wrote with his own hand a letter of friendship to the king of the Greeks, setting out the borders and dealing with the return of Sicily [?].
He gave up Philistia, with the territory of Jerusalem. And he said: "Jerusalem is the city of your faith."

And he gave Gorgasali gifts: three thousand litras of aloe wood, five hundred litras of ambergris, five hundred litras of musk, three thousand Arabian horses, a thousand Khosrovian garments, and three thousand khazd [?].
And Vakhtang went home. The next day the king sent Barzaban to King Vakhtang,
his own mobidan, and said this to Gorgasali: "I will now do whatever you want from me. Govern your realm as you wish.
"Send officials and take over your cities, the ones I have given to you and to the emperor.
"And I have ordered Barzaban to go to the emperor to hand over your lands and cities. But you know that the Persian elders have become angry with us over this matter,
"because they thought that I would crush the land of the Greeks, but today I have given away two kingdoms from my own territory.
"Now this is my request: that you give me your sister as a wife, and that you come with me to the land of our fathers,

"so that you may see your kinsmen, and so that you may help me in person against my enemies, the Abyssinians and the Elamites, the Indians and the Sindhis, because they have done the worst evil to my kingship and humiliated it.
"Now when you come with me, I will say this to my elders and my marzpans: that I made this friendship of mine and of my friends because my brother King Vakhtang wished it so.
"With the help of the very lands we have given away, we will make our enemies pay tribute to us, and in this way we will calm their anger against the Greeks.
"But you yourself, agree to come in person as a force to aid me, while your troops stay where they are."
Then Vakhtang summoned his counsellors, and Leo the anthypatos (proconsul) spoke thus:
"Great is the good you have done to the Greeks, greater than that of the kings who sit on their thrones,
for you protected the city of Pontus from destruction, and you granted seven hundred and eighty thousand souls, and today it is being given through you.
"Jazira and Philistia, which no king of the Greeks has held in peace. And Khosrow is right that if you do not do him a kindness in return, his people will consider him worthless.
"Even though he did not ask it of you, let us go beyond [?] what he asks, because this is perfect friendship.
"I will give you ten thousand armoured men from my army, and I will go with your envoys before the emperor, and from there I will join you in Jazira with a powerful army."
This is what Leo the proconsul advised. And his counsel pleased King Vakhtang and all his nobles.
King Vakhtang gave his sister, named Mirandukht, to the king of the Persians as a wife. She had been taken captive by the Ossetians, and Vakhtang had freed her.
He did not give Khuarandze, because she was betrothed to the patiakhsh (viceroy) of the Armenians.
Vakhtang brought his son, who was called Darchil in Persian and Dachi in Georgian.
The boy was five years old. Vakhtang crowned him, left him as king, and left seven of his nobles with him:
first, Juansher the spaspet (commander-in-chief), who held Inner Kartli and had authority over all the eristavis (dukes); and Demetre, eristavi of Kakheti and Kukheti;
Grigol, eristavi of Hereti; Nersaran, eristavi of Khunani; and Adarnase, eristavi of Samshvilde;
Samnaghir, eristavi of Inner Egrisi and Svaneti; and Bakur, eristavi of Margvi and Takveri.
He entrusted his son Dachi to these men. He ordered them to build Ujarma and to raise King Dachi there,
for he had found it well suited for game and for flocks. He took four of his nobles with him:
Artavaz, eristavi of Klarjeti; Nasar, eristavi of Tsunda; Bivritian, eristavi of Odzrkhe;
and Saurmag, his great ejibi (chamberlain). With them went ten thousand chosen horsemen of his army.
Leon the anthypatos left ten thousand Greeks from his army and went himself before the emperor.
King Vakhtang sent Artavaz, eristavi of Klarjeti, with him as an envoy. He sent to the emperor all the gifts that had been bestowed by King Khosrow,
