except that he kept the brocades (stavra) and the Arabian horses for himself. He sent everything else, and he ordered Artavaz to join Leon the anthypatos at Jazira.
Vakhtang's mother and his sister Khuarandze begged him to take them with him so that they could pray in Jerusalem.
He took them with him. King Vakhtang and Khosrow went by the road through Adarbadagan (Azerbaijan). From there Vakhtang, his mother and his sister went to Jerusalem, while Khosrow waited at Antioch.

They entered and prayed at the holy Resurrection (the Church of the Holy Sepulchre). They visited and prayed at all the holy places, entrusted themselves to the holy Resurrection, and made a great offering. Then they came back to Antioch.
Leon, the emperor's anthypatos, and Artavaz, Vakhtang's eristavi, came with twenty thousand chosen horsemen.
From the emperor they brought Khosrow an incomparable present and Vakhtang an incomparable gift.
Through the envoys the emperor had sent word of his joy and his thanksgiving to God, and of his boundless praise and gratitude to Vakhtang. He sent this message to Vakhtang:
"I have ordered Leon to stand in awe of you and be under your command as he is under mine." Fifty thousand chosen horsemen, Greek, Georgian and Armenian, gathered under Vakhtang's command.
Then the king of the Persians said to Vakhtang: "Since your mother and your sister have traveled this far, let them also come to my kingdom,
so that we may celebrate our joy together. Afterward, if they wish to go to Kartli, let them go by the road through Ran.
But if they wish to wait for you, let them wait for you in the city of Urha (Edessa)." Khosrow's command pleased Vakhtang. So they took the women with them and set out.
The king of the Persians sent an envoy to all the nobles of Persia and told them all of this.
And they rejoiced with great joy, for they burned like fire to fight against the Indians, the Sindians, the Abyssinians and the Jurjanians.
And they came to Baghdad, and all the nobles of Persia came out to meet them with great joy.
And they held the royal wedding for six months, with delight and with ease beyond compare.
And after the wedding he gave a very great gift to Vakhtang's mother and sister, and they set out for Uraha [?].
And all the people of Persia honored Vakhtang as they honored Khosrow, their king. And then they marched against the enemies.
Here: Vakhtang Gorgasali's help to the king of the Persians against the Indians, the Sindians,
the Abyssinians and the Jurjanians, and Vakhtang's victory over them all. First they went to Jurjan, and they plundered Jurjan and left it wholly without inhabitants.
And in their place they settled people of Persian stock. And from then on the Jurjanians became peasants, and they are now tributaries of the Persians.
Vakhtang Gorgasali's entry into India and Vakhtang's victory over them. And from there they entered India, and there fierce battles took place, and single combats.
And the custom there was this: whichever of them won, the camp would flee before him.
And King Vakhtang killed fifteen champions there, who had struck down many Persian giants.
And they spent three years in the war in India, and they plundered most of the lands of India. But they could not destroy the strong fortress-cities, because the people stayed within the walls.
And they took tribute from the king of the Indians: a thousand litras of musk, the same amount of ambergris, ten shiploads of aloe-wood,
one shipload of gems, jacinth and emerald, and with it sapphires of every kind, a hundred camel-loads of gold, and five hundred camel-loads of silver.
Vakhtang Gorgasali's entry into Sind and Vakhtang's victory. And from there they entered Sind.
Then the king of the Sindians divided his people among the fortresses and cities. And in whatever district the Persians went out to plunder,
the Sindians would sally out against them from the fortresses and cities and inflict great harm on the Persians, and countless Persians were killed.
But by the power of Christ, Vakhtang's troops were defeated nowhere, and they proved victorious over the enemies in every way.
And Vakhtang's four nobles and Leo the Greek proved to be brave fighters,
for they struck down many of the brave fighting champions of the Sindians. And the king of the Sindians was in the city of Sindia.
Then they went with all their forces to Sindia, and fierce battles took place there. And every day the king of the Sindians himself would come out,
for he was a brave and daring giant, and he would bring out the horsemen of Sind, and there would be battles of champions. On some days these won, and on other days those.
And the king of the Sindians overcame, by his own hand, all the champions who fought against him. And for many days he and Vakhtang did not meet in battle.
Then at night the king of the Sindians dug a great pit on the field before the gates of the city, to hide horsemen inside it,
and he skilfully left passages for them to come out, and he placed ten chosen horsemen in it.
Early in the morning he sent out a champion. That day it was Vakhtang's turn to guard the gates.
This champion rode up and challenged him to single combat, intending to lure him away and draw him onto those horsemen.
Then Saurmag, Vakhtang's chamberlain, went out and said: "You are not bold enough to fight the king. I will fight you instead, servant against servant." And he attacked.
But the Sindian fled, and Saurmag chased him as he usually did, because he had fought many times on that field.
As he rode past the hidden horsemen, they burst out behind him, and the man who had fled turned back.
Saurmag struck the man in front of him with his spear and killed him, but those ten killed Saurmag.
Then King Vakhtang himself attacked, and with him his three nobles, Artavaz, Bivritian and Nasar, and Leon the Greek with them.
The Sindians fled, and Vakhtang chased them, cutting them down, all the way to the gates of the city, and the Sindians fled into the city.
Then Vakhtang returned full of grief and mourned over Saurmag's body as if over a beloved brother.
For Saurmag was his foster-brother, the nephew of his foster-father, who was Artavaz's father. He was loyal, trustworthy and brave.
The fable of the king of the Sindians. Then the king of the Sindians stood at the city gates and called out in a loud voice, saying:
"King Vakhtang, you are like the foolish crow that found a hawk wounded and torn by an eagle. The hawk could not fly and was close to death.
That crow did not do what crows normally do.
Any other crow, when it sees a hawk, starts cawing loudly and lets the others hear too, and a crowd of crows falls upon the hawk,
to drive it away from their homes so that they can live their days without fear. Even dumb animals know what is good for them.
"That crow did nothing like this. Instead it took pity on the hawk as if the hawk were its benefactor.
It stopped feeding its own chicks and kept gathering locusts and snakes, because a crow cannot catch anything else, and with these it fed the hawk.
When the hawk's wings had grown back, it said to itself:
"For many days now I have been fed on locusts and snakes, and they have not given me the strength my parents had, because I cannot grow strong on locusts.
If only I had the strength to catch birds and feed myself that way! Instead I will seize that crow that raised me, eat it, and rest for two days.
Then my strength will return, and I will go off to hunt as is our custom, like our fathers did."
So it did this: it seized the crow and ate it. From then on it began to hunt large and swift birds.
The crow was given no praise for its mercy. Instead it is called foolish and its own killer.
Nor was the hawk blamed for being merciless and ungrateful, because that is

the nature and custom of the hawk. It was wasting away and dying on locusts, so it acted according to its custom and was saved from death. The crow, however, did not act according to custom, and that is why it died.
"Now the Persians, who from the beginning until now and onward to eternity are enemies of the worshippers of the Cross, show love with flattery in a time of weakness;
but when the time comes, they show no mercy and no remembrance of kindness. We have heard from books that this has happened countless times.
And when you saw the Persians brought low by me, you did not do what you should have done: rejoice and offer thanks to your God,
and also counsel other nations, stir up enemies against the Persians, and help the enemies of Persia.
You did nothing of the kind. Instead, you have left the dwelling of your fathers and become the leader of the great Christian army of the Greeks, and you have travelled a road of two years,
and you have come as a strength to the Persians, so that they may grow strong and gain respite, and then destroy you and your land, and take hold of it to destroy all the worshippers of the Cross.
Truly you are preparing this for yourself and for all the worshippers of the Cross. Why should I tell the fable of the crow about you?
For you are a sovereign and valiant king, and of your own will you have given yourself as a slave to your enemies. So how can I not call you foolish?"
The Discourse of Vakhtang Gorgasali. Then Vakhtang said to him: "You thought that what you said was devised with wisdom, but those words of yours are false.
I will tell you and make the truth known to you: fool, you are like the burrowing mouse, the mole, which has no eyes, and whose dwelling
is under the earth. It does not know the brightness of the sun or the beauty of the fields, and it is content with its own life, for it thinks that this is all there is.
It thinks the life of all moving creatures [?] is the same as the life it lives itself, and it has no desire to see the light and the beauty of heaven and earth.
"In the same way, you are blind in the eye of the mind and deaf in the ear of the mind: you do not see, you do not hear, and you do not know the spiritual life;
nor do you desire to go to that eternal life, that endless light, that inconceivable and unattainable glory.
Nor do you know God, the Creator of all, through whom all things were made.
"I have not come to this land for the glory of this world, nor to serve the king of the Persians,
but to serve God who is without beginning, the Trinity of one essence, the Creator of all, for the sake of the endless glory of the age to come.
For by my coming here I have first of all delivered Jerusalem, the holy city, where the feet of our Lord Jesus Christ stood, and where he accomplished everything for the salvation of our souls.
And after that I have saved all of Christendom from devastation, for the king of the Persians had been granted a time to plunder all of Christendom.
"Even though my own land would have been protected by the power of Christ and the courage of my troops, the Greeks were occupied and could not resist. And so it is right for us who believe in Christ
to lay down our lives for even one of our neighbours. Yet countless souls have been saved by my coming here,
and I have done this so that God the Creator may accept this service of mine and lighten my sins.
And as for what you said, 'Once the Persians are at peace, they will become enemies of the Christians': by the power and help of Christ, I have now saved the Christians from great affliction,
And afterwards God the Creator again showed mercy to those who trusted in him.
"Even if there had been no cause in the deliverance of the Christians, I would still have come here myself as a force for the Persians.
This too was right, first for the sake of kinship, and then for this reason: although the Persians are not of the true faith,
yet they know God the Creator and believe in spiritual life. But you are wholly ignorant of God and without understanding, like the horse and the mule.
How then would God, the Creator of all things, not accept this as service? And even judging by the affairs of this passing world, your mind is detestable.
For you praise the deed of the treacherous hawk that ate the crow which had reared it. But this is our nature:
that we lay down our life for our benefactor, and gain grace from God, and find eternal life,
and in this world gain praise from men. And if we die for the name of God and for his commandments, we are immortal, and we pass from death into life."
Then the king of Sind said: "Long debate between us is useless. But as for what you said, that if I die for the name of my God,
I pass from death into life: well then, if a man knows the glory and good that are coming to him, it is right that he should hasten to reach that kingdom.
Now therefore I know truly that you are going to the kingdom. Come out to fight me, so that by my hand you may pass today from death into life;
for that nobleman of yours has been sent on ahead as your forerunner, to prepare your dwelling place for you."
Vakhtang said: "I do not count death now as joy, for I am a sinner, and I have not fully kept the commandment of God,
and I have not fully wiped out my sins by repentance. But by the power of Christ I do not fear death from you;
for he is my protector, by whom I am kept safe in all things. And may the all-merciful God, by the great power that comes from him,
kill you, his blasphemer, by the hand of me, his servant, and may your soul go into the outer darkness, into the fire that is never quenched."
Then the king of the Sinds came out, and Vakhtang said to his companions:
"Pray to God, and guard my side at my back." And Vakhtang went out, and both of them had spears.
Then they began to ride around the field in a circle, and both sought a way to strike with the point of the spear.
Then the king of Sind timed his move to get past the point of Vakhtang's spear and charged at him to strike him with his spear.
But with the courage and agility of his body Vakhtang swerved from the spear and escaped it, wheeled around like a whirlwind, and struck the king of Sind with his spear in the left shoulder.
The strength of his armour did not protect him, and he was badly wounded, for the spear came out a cubit's length through the front.
And the king of Sind fell down, and Vakhtang went up to him, reached down and seized him by the foot, and dragged him before the king of the Persians.
Then the whole army praised Vakhtang with a loud voice, and the king of the Persians and his whole camp were filled with joy.
And all the nobles came before King Vakhtang with gifts and presented their gifts.

Then the king of the Persians brought a skilled physician and put him in charge of the king of Sind, so that he might be healed of his wound, and so that through him the Persian king might take all of Sind.
But the Sindians set up his son as king in place of their king.
Then King Vakhtang advised the king of the Persians to release the king of the Sindians and to take tribute and hostages, because they could not hold Sindia.

The king of the Persians was pleased with Vakhtang's advice. He released the king of the Sindians and took from him twice as much tribute as he had taken from the Indians, and two of his children as hostages.
The king of the Persians gave all this tribute of the Sindians to Vakhtang. Then that king of the Sindians became devoted to Vakhtang with great love:
first, because when he fell into Vakhtang's hands, Vakhtang did not kill him but brought him alive before the king of the Persians;
and second, because it was through Vakhtang that he was set free from captivity. And he gave Vakhtang an immeasurably great quantity of gifts.
And they came away from Sindia in the fourth year after entering Sindia. The cities of Sindia that remained unravaged were Sindila, Topori and Kimrai.
Here: the entry of the king of the Persians and Vakhtang Gorgasali into Abyssinia, and its capture by them. And from there they came to Abyssinia.
Now the Abyssinians were settled in a land surrounded by water and reed beds, where no boat could travel
and no four-footed animal either. It lies on the borders of Persia. And they fought with patient endurance.
For they diverted the water that flowed into it, burned the reed beds with fire, and carried off all Abyssinia captive.

And the king of the Persians divided the Abyssinians in two. He left half of them in their own place and brought away the other half, about a thousand households, and scattered them from place to place.
And these are the Kurds, the people whom they carried off captive from the Abyssinians.
And in the eighth year after entering Persia, Vakhtang came away as far as Antioch and arrived at Urha [Edessa].
And the king of the Persians was offering Vakhtang a wife from among his royal kin. But Vakhtang said:
"It is not permitted to me to have two wives, for I have as my wife the daughter of Caesar."
This displeased King Khosrow, but he could not say anything. Vakhtang found his mother and his sister in peace, and they came as far as the border between the Greeks and the Armenians.
Leo the Greek and his army went to Shimshat [Samosata]. Vakhtang sent a messenger to bring his wife, and also for Peter the catholicos and Samuel the bishop.
Vakhtang came to Kartli. His son Dachi came to meet him, and with him all the commanders, and the bishops with them.
When the bishop learned that the king had sent a messenger to bring the catholicos and the bishops, he was offended by it.
And he began [?] to revolt and to seek pretexts, and he sent to the king and said:
"You have abandoned Christ and trust in fire." But Vakhtang sent word back:
"By the power of Christ I went in, and in righteousness I came out, by the power of Christ as well, and I am innocent; God knows. But I have sent an envoy to bring the catholicos and the bishops."
When the bishop heard this, he held firm in his purpose. He hoped to stir up trouble to delay that matter and their coming, and he anathematized the king and all his troops.
But the king said: "Even though we are innocent, it is right for us to be humble." The king went, and he got down from his horse so that he could fall at the bishop's feet.
And he moved his foot and struck the king in the mouth with his shoe, and broke his tooth.
But the king said: "This insolence of arrogance is a snare of the devil;
if the multitude of my sins has provoked you, you do not have authority to do evil, but to forgive, as the Gospel says:
'You shall not quench a burning wick, nor break a bruised reed.'"
"But you think that by your treachery you might make us give up the love of Christ.
It became plainly evident then, when you heard that one superior to you was being brought to Kartli, and you were inflamed with wicked envy, as Judas was with envy of Peter;
for you are like Judas, and the Church is like Peter. You are a lover of silver, for you too are a betrayer [?] of Christ.
Now I will send you to the patriarch at Constantinople, and let him judge you as is fitting."
And he sent him with envoys, and his tooth with him, and sent word that they should quickly send a catholicos and twelve bishops,
and that among them Peter should be catholicos and Samuel a bishop, and the others whoever they pleased. And when they brought Bishop Michael there, the patriarch said to him:
"Since blood has been shed on the ground by you, you are no longer worthy to be a bishop, and for your insolence toward the king you deserve death, as it says:
'Submit yourselves to kings, for they do not gird on the sword in vain, for the king rules by God, like a lion among sheep.'"
And they exiled Bishop Michael to the monastery of the Sleepless Ones. And they sent Peter the priest and Samuel the monk to Antioch.
And the emperor and the patriarch of Constantinople wrote to the patriarch of Antioch as follows:
"At first, at the beginning of the conversion of Kartli by the Roman woman Nino, a bishop was sent from here,
because there was strife between the Persians and the Greeks, and for that reason they could not carry out this matter as the canon law requires;
for we know that Kartli and the East and the North belong to that holy see of yours, as the apostles ordained in the Gospel, which is the primacy." And they wrote to him
the whole affair of the great King Vakhtang, saying: "The bishop who had been appointed by them we have deposed, and know that today Kartli is truly newly planted.
Now consecrate these two whom they have requested, and the other twelve, whomever you wish, consecrate them.
And let them come to us, so that we may send them off with gifts and every provision."
And the patriarch of Antioch consecrated twelve bishops, and Peter as catholicos.

And they came to Constantinople, and the emperor gave them a great many gifts, and he gave his daughter, named Helena, to King Vakhtang, and sent her off with a large army as far as the borders of Armenia.
And King Vakhtang met her there, and the Greek troops turned back. And they went on to Mtskheta.

And in Mtskheta King Vakhtang built the Church of the Apostles, Sveti Tskhoveli [the Living Pillar], and within the Pillar church, on the south side, he kept the place where the church had collapsed, which is the Great Sion.
And there they installed Peter as catholicos and Samuel as bishop of the same episcopal see of Mtskheta.
And he appointed one as bishop in Klarjeti, at the church of Akhiza; one in Artani, at Erusheti; one in Javakheti, at Tsunda; one at Manglisi; one at Bolnisi;
one at Rustavi; one at Ninotsminda, at the gate of Ujarma, which Gorgasali had built;
one at Cheremi, which he had also built, and there he made a city between the two churches, which he himself had built;
one at Cheleti, which [?] village and built [?]; one at Khornabuji; and one at Agaraki, which is opposite Khunani.
After this he built the church of Nikozi beside the fire-temple.
And he appointed a bishop where the body of Saint Razhden was buried; Razhden had been martyred by the Persians during Vakhtang's war.
This Razhden was the foster-father of Vakhtang's wife, the daughter of the king of the Persians, whom Vakhtang had married first. Razhden converted to Christianity and became a man of great faith.
He fought mightily in that battle. The Persians captured him and tried to force him to deny Christ.
But the saint chose that unfading glory and was martyred for Christ. And Vakhtang had three sons and two daughters by his Greek wife.
To Dachi, his firstborn son by his first wife, he gave the city of Cheremi and Nekresi,
and the city of Kambechovani, which is Khornabuji, and all the land east of the Mtkvari.
Vakhtang himself settled at Ujarma and built it up with immense buildings. And he gave his sister Khvarandze as wife to Bakur, the patiakhsh (viceroy) of Armenia.
When some time had passed in this way, Khosrow, king of the Persians, died, and his son Khosrow took the throne in his place.
The Persians had grown strong, because all their enemies had been subdued through Vakhtang's campaign. Khosrow set out to make war on the Greeks, and he sent an envoy to Gorgasali, saying:
"My father died, and all his people made me king on his thrones, and my elders commanded me thus:
that I should come before you and obey your command, and that you, O king, should lead us as our leader in this entry of ours into the land of the Greeks.
And give me your daughter as my wife, so that I may be like one of your own children."
When the envoy came before King Vakhtang, Vakhtang was building the city of Tbilisi and had only laid its foundation.
When the envoy delivered King Khosrow's message [?], the king said: "This is why they say: 'Smith, sharpen your sword, so that it may soon be weighed against
your limbs." At that time Vakhtang was advanced in days, about sixty years old, and he spoke thus:
"Tell King Khosrow: first prepare for battle with us, and then enter the land of the Greeks, for the mighty deeds that have been done were all done by the power of the Cross.
Now let our life rest on hope in the Crucified One." And he sent out a herald ordering the people to abandon the villages and cities
that were not strongly fortified and to flee into the Caucasus and into Kakheti, for Kakheti was forest and impenetrable to an enemy.

King Dachi and his sister's son crossed over into Kakheti and stationed themselves in the gorge of the Lopota, a land walled in by cliffs. The people of that region were worshippers of fire and water,
and that gorge was filled with a multitude of people as far as Nosra, while Gorgasali's wife and children were in the gorge of Ujarma.
And he himself took his stand at the front fortress, and with him Juansher and Adarnase.
But he left Demetre and Nerse and Bivritiani at Mtskheta. He sent a messenger and informed the Emperor.

Here: the coming of the Persians to Kartli to make war on Vakhtang Gorgasali; the killing by Vakhtang of Bartam, son of the Persian king; and how King Khosro came and destroyed the city of Kambechovani, the fortress of Cheremi, and Veli-tsikhe.
And when they reached Kakheti, they camped on the Iori. Vakhtang's troops took up position on the plain around the fortress-city called Darphaka.
And they clashed on the Iori and fought every day for three days, and countless men fell on both sides.
Then Vakhtang summoned Catholicos Peter and said: "Know that they are fighting us not over the payment of tribute, but so that we will abandon Christ.
Now I have resolved this: death for the name of Christ is better than my life, so that we may have the Kingdom promised to be shared with those to whom he says:
"whoever loses his life for my sake will find it." Peter the Catholicos said to him:
"You have seen things that none of your kin has seen: help that comes from Christ.
For in your wisdom you know that the enemy who tempts us disputes with God over us, as he did over Job;
for God permits this so that those he hates are destroyed, but those he loves are deified.
Do as God counsels you. Even if you do not die, we will die." With these words he revealed that he would not survive that battle, and he said:
"Not only will Kartli be given over to destruction, but Jerusalem too, which is the mother of all the children of light." And the king said:
"Stay in the church of Saint Razhden, which I have built in the suburb of Ujarma; and I hope that all the towns around Ujarma
will be overcome, for it is here that we have built strong and mighty walls." And the catholicos did so.
And all the holy bishops gathered there. Vakhtang's army numbered two hundred and forty thousand, and the Persians' seven hundred and forty thousand.
And Vakhtang divided his army into three. He sent the infantry along the side of the cliff; on another side he sent the pitiakhshes and the commander-in-chief (spaspet);
and Vakhtang himself, with about one hundred thousand troops, advanced against the place where the Persian king was.
At night, just as the dawn was breaking through the mist, Vakhtang fell upon the Persians, and he said to all his people:
"Any man who escapes death but does not bring back the head or the hand of one of our enemies will be put to death by us."
And as dawn was breaking, he attacked and broke through all the way to the king's pavilion.
He entered the king's tent, and the king escaped on horseback. Vakhtang killed the king's son Bartam and cut off his head.
And there a certain Persian shot an arrow into Vakhtang's chest. The battle went on until midday.
Vakhtang defeated those Persians and killed about one hundred and thirty thousand of them, while about twenty-eight thousand of Vakhtang's troops died.
And they carried off about one hundred thousand captured horses. Because there were so many of them, they could not completely rout them.
And the king of the Persians moved on from there and encamped at Rustavi. And Vakhtang's wound grew grave, for the arrow had pierced his lung.
And he went to Ujarma, and ordered the commanders of the army of Kartli to stay where they were.
The Persians learned that Vakhtang's wound had brought him low, and they laid waste to Tbilisi and Armazi in Kartli.
But they could not take Mtskheta. They only laid waste to what lay outside the wall, at Mukhnari and at the confluence of the Aragvi.
Meanwhile the king of the Greeks, Vakhtang's father-in-law, died, and his son Zeno became king. And he set out for Speri, to come on to Kartli.
And when he learned how gravely ill Vakhtang was, he halted at the city of Karnu. And Khosrow came there, and Khosrow and the Caesar fought each other at Karnipora.
And so many were killed on both sides that a river of blood was formed. Because of this the place was called Karnipora, that is, "belly of blood."
And neither could defeat the other, for the armies of both were cut down. And Khosrow turned back along the road to Kartli.
But Vakhtang knew that he was going to die, and he summoned the catholicos, his wife, his sons and all the nobles, and said:
"I am now departing to stand before my God, and I give thanks to his name, for he has not ranked me below his chosen saints.
Now I command you to stand firm in the faith and to seek death for Christ, for the sake of his name, so that you may win glory that never fades."
And he said to all the nobles: "You, the inhabitants of Kartli, remember the good I have done you,
for it was first through my house that you received the eternal light, and I raised you, my kinsfolk, to earthly glory.
Do not hold our house in contempt, and do not give up your friendship with the Greeks." And he said to his son Dachi:
"You are my firstborn son. To you I have given the crown of my kingship. And as their portion I have given your brothers the land from Tasiskari and Tsunda as far as Armenia and Greece,
and the borderland of Abkhazia, which lies between the Egris-tsqali river and Klisura. That land belongs to your brothers'
own mother. Let them have it, and let them be eristavis (dukes) for you, in obedience to your line.
And he summoned Nasar, the eristavi of Tsunda, Artavaz, the eristavi of Klarjeti, and Bivritian, the eristavi of Odzrkhe,
and entrusted to them his wife Helena and her sons, who were named Leon and Mirdat. With tears, and with his eyes raised to God, he commended them to all three eristavis.
Then for the nobles and all the people it was a day of judgment. They all beat themselves and poured ashes on their heads, and every one of them longed for his own death.
And the earth shook with the sound of weeping and lamentation. And the faithful people called the king blessed, because he had been killed for Christ.
And Vakhtang died and was buried in Mtskheta, in the catholicos's church, beside the column that holds [?] part taken from the God-raised pillar.
And on his tomb his image is painted, life-size.
And now his armor and garments, which still exist, make him [?] even better known. The thirty-fourth king: Dachi, son of Vakhtang Gorgasali.
A Khosroid. And his son Dachi took his throne. But those three eristavis took Vakhtang's wife and two sons away with them, and they held the west of Kartli,
…which Vakhtang had given. And they settled in the city of Tsunda in summer, and in winter they would stay at Odzrkhe.
And they were not called kings, but chief of the eristavis, and they were subject to their brother, King Dachi.
This King Dachi began to rebuild Kartli, for all the valleys of Kartli had been laid waste, except Kakheti, Klarjeti and Egrisi.
And he completed the walls of Tbilisi and, as Vakhtang had commanded, made it the royal residence.
And Catholicos Peter died, and Samuel took his seat. And the king entrusted Mtskheta to him, for so King Vakhtang had commanded.
This same King Dachi called on the mountain people of Kakheti to confess Christ, but they refused, and all the Nopateli [?] rebelled.
Of the two sons of Vakhtang born of his Greek wife, the one called Leon died, and only Mirdat remained.
His brother, King Dachi, made a bargain with this Mirdat: the king exchanged lands with him, and took from Mirdat the land between the Egris-tsqali and Klisura,
the border land of Greece that Mirdat had inherited from his mother, and gave him Javakheti in exchange, from Paravani to the Mtkvari.
Mirdat, son of Vakhtang, held the land from Paravani and Tasiskari as far as the sea of Speri, and ruled there as eristavi;
and he was subject to King Dachi, his brother. He built the church of Tsqarostavi in Javakheti. And King Dachi died.
The thirty-fifth king, Bakur, son of King Dachi, a Khosroid. And his son Bakur took his seat as king. And Bakur died.
The thirty-sixth king, Parsman, son of King Bakur, a Khosroid. And his son Parsman took his seat as king. And Catholicos Samuel died, and Tavpechag became catholicos.
And Tavpechag died, and Chermag became catholicos. From Vakhtang until this time these kings lived in peace, and the children of Mirdat served the children of Dachi.
In the reign of this Parsman the Persians came and laid waste Kartli and Ran.
But Parsman, king of the Georgians, asked the king of the Persians not to lay waste the churches, and to let Kartli keep the law of Christ.
For at that time the Greeks were occupied elsewhere: enemies had risen up against them in the west, and they could not help the Georgians or stand against the Persians.
Then the king of the Persians heard his plea and spared the churches. And Parsman pledged to him in writing his obedience and service, and the king of the Persians went away.
From that time the descendants of King Vakhtang were divided, for the children of Dachi were subject to the Persians, while the children of Mirdat remained subject to the Greeks.
Parsman died, and his nephew, who was also called Parsman, took his seat as king. The thirty-seventh king, Parsman.
The nephew of King Parsman, a Khosroid. He was a believer like his uncle, and he added to the adornment of all the churches.
And the Georgians asked Justinian that men of Georgian birth be appointed catholicos.
For the catholicoi used to come from Greece. And Justinian wrote a letter and sealed it with his own seal, ordering
that men of Georgian birth be appointed catholicos, and that they have authority over all the churches and bishops.
And Catholicos Chermag died, and this same King Parsman appointed Saba.
From then on they no longer brought the catholicos from Greece. Instead Georgians took the seat, men from the families of the nobility.
Catholicos Saba died, and that same king appointed Evlati as catholicos.
In the time of this same Parsman, John came from Mesopotamia. He was called John of Zedazeni, the enlightener of Kartli and purifier of the faith,
the builder of churches. He and his disciples worked many miracles and signs, at which all the Georgians marveled.
Their lives and miracles were written down and placed in the churches of Kartli.
The names of the holy disciples: John of Zedazeni, David of Gareja, Stephen of Khirsa, Joseph of Alaverdi, Zenon of Iqalto, Anthony the Solitary,
Ise of Tsilkani, Tate of Stepantsminda, Shio of Mghvime, Isidore of Samtavisi, Abibos of Nekresi, Michael of Ulumbo, Piros of Breti, and Elias the Deacon.

Many others also became disciples of that holy father: holy men and spiritual fathers [?] of that time. Four hundred and twenty years later, our holy father Arsenius, Catholicos of Kartli, inquired and investigated,
and some of it we read in books, and some of it had been heard about their deeds.
We have written down the life and conduct of those holy fathers, so that we believers may know of them and to the glory of the Holy Trinity,
now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen. Now let us begin their life in brief.
John was from the land of Mesopotamia. We do not know his parents. Only the heavenly Father do we know as his parent.
He grew up and became accomplished in all learning, and he was adorned with perfect virtue.
For this reason God granted him the healing of diseases and the driving out of demons, and through this gift many miracles were performed.
Since he suffered much grief, he fled to the desert and stayed there.
There he received a command through an angel to go to Kartli with his twelve disciples.
He came to Mtskheta, and by the command of the king and with the blessing of the catholicos he went up onto the mountain of Zedazeni,
and he settled there in seclusion. From of old idols had been set up on that mountain, and because of this a multitude of demons dwelt there.
But through the prayers of the holy father John, all of them were driven from that mountain.
He sent out his disciples under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, some to Kartli, some to Kakheti, and some to the desert of Gareja.
Then John, our venerable father, remained there with only one disciple. They endured much opposition and many trials from the devil, and they showed themselves victorious over all of them.

After this, through his prayer, God brought forth a sweet spring on that waterless mountain. Many sick people from among the common folk were healed by drinking its water and anointing themselves with it.
After this, with gentle instruction, he drove away a bear that stood guard over that spring;
and from then until the present day the bears of that mountain have never again harmed any person.
Thus the bears were tamed without a shepherd [?]. They brought him a man who had been paralysed for a long time, and through his prayer he was healed at once.
Then they brought another man, who had a demon of muteness. He prayed for him, and at once the demon left him and fled from him.
And that man was healed and glorified God. Of his many miracles we have told these few.
When the time came for him to depart from the body, he called Elias the deacon and some others of his disciples, and he taught them and strengthened them.
And he saw the heavenly hosts come to him, and he committed his soul into their hands and fell asleep in peace.
They anointed his holy body with myrrh and laid it in his own dwelling, on that same mountain where he had struggled.
After his death many miracles were performed, and the full Life of Saint John tells of them.
The holy father David was from the land of Mesopotamia. We do not know who his parents were.
He came as a disciple with John, and he went out into the desert of Gareja with only one disciple, whose name was Lucian.
They endured a great many heats of the sun and frosts of winter. After this they were fed by deer, like the father of Basil the Great.
For three deer with their fawns would come, and they would milk them and eat the curds made from the milk. But on Wednesdays and Fridays the deer would not come.
After a short time one of the fawns was swallowed by a fierce dragon that lived in a certain ravine, in the clefts of the rock.
At David's word the dragon was driven away, and on the plain of Karaia it was burned up by a thunderbolt. And Bubakar, a nobleman, while hunting partridges,
came upon the saint and wanted to kill him with a sword. The hand he had stretched out withered. Then, at the same saint's prayer, it was restored and was as if it had never been harmed.
Bubakar's sons were lame, and the saint healed them in an instant by his prayer.
Because of this his fame spread, and a great many people became his disciples, and they carved out many caves.
The venerable Dodo also came and stayed with him.
After this the saint made bitter waters sweet. These waters still flow to this day around the monastery of Bertubani. And he performed many miracles.
Afterwards the saint went to the holy city of Jerusalem on foot. When he reached the place where the city can be seen from the hills, he did not allow himself to go down into it.
Instead, from there he bowed down and worshipped. He picked up three stones, put them into some kind of pouch [?], and set out on his way back.
Because of this the patriarch saw a vision. He sent swift runners, who caught up with the saint. They took two of the stones from him and let him keep one.
He came back and brought that stone. The wonders of the stone had been told to the patriarch by an angel: the three stones were not to be given away,
but a third of the grace of the holy city was to be brought here to the desert, since praying here three times is equal to going to Jerusalem once.
After this he committed his soul to God, and his holy body was laid in his own dwelling, the monastery of Gareja.
His miracles and his struggles are written down in full in his complete Life.
While this holy father David was still alive, the holy father Dodo came from Kakheti. With the blessing of that same holy father he went out from there into the desert and settled there,
And he built a very great monastery, in which he accomplished many struggles and labours.
His miracles, life and struggle are related to us by his Life.
And after this he commended his soul to God, and his holy body was laid in his own dwelling.
The holy father Shio was from the city of Antioch. From childhood he had left the world and become a disciple of father John.
When holy John came to Kartli, led by the divine Spirit, the venerable Shio did not abandon his spiritual father, and came along with him.
Having come to Kartli, to the city of Mtskheta, he longed for quiet and solitude.
He asked leave of the Catholicos and of father John, and holy Shio went to the west of Mtskheta, on the right of the river Mtkvari,
to the place called Mghvime ("the Cave"), among very deep ravines. His flesh was cracked by the heat of the sun and the frosts of winter.
He found a cave hewn out of the rock, and in it he found relief from the cold and the heat.
And since the good God did not overlook his many struggles, just as he fed Elijah by a raven, so here too food was brought to him day by day by a dove.
After this, one day, a rich and prominent man named Evagrius came out to hunt with birds.
Standing alone on the top of a cliff, he saw a dove carrying food. He watched it closely and wondered at it in his mind. And again on the second day he saw the same thing

as before, and he followed the track of the dove. He found an elder engaged in ascetic struggle, and he sought to emulate that elder's endurance and did not disregard his own separation [from the world] [?]. He said: "Father, make me worthy
to live with you, so that I may finish my days in quiet." Holy Shio said to him:
"Take this staff of mine. If the river makes a way for you, from that side and from this, and the water parts, it is the will of the Lord, and come here.
And if no way is made for you, be a household and [?] willing and trustworthy [?]." He went off, departing from the household [?], like Moses.
Twice that staff parted the Mtkvari. Evagrius went up to father Shio without looking back, as Lot did from Sodom, and he was not turned into a pillar of salt through fear.
He taught him patience, prayer, keeping vigil and the struggle of the monastic life. After this, Saint Shio said:
"My son Evagrius, we need a church; wherever the Lord wills, let us, suppliants of God, go up [?]."
On the top of the edge of the cliff he put incense and fire in his left hand, and with his right he made the sign of the cross.
By the smoke of the incense turning down at the edge, the place where the Lord willed a church was found, and he built a church of the all-holy Mother of God.
Evagrius became a monk. The story of them spread, and from all the surrounding villages others came, countless souls, to become monks.
All food, and water too, had to be carried there. They had donkeys to carry the loads. He gave orders to the wolves, and the wolves stood as herdsmen over the donkeys.
One day the donkey of the elder Conon fell from the cliff and did not come back to the stable.
That elder said to holy Shio: "What is this that I have done [?], that you appointed a wolf as herdsman of the donkeys? It has eaten this one."

The wolf had been in the habit, whenever it led off the karauli [?], of scattering the monks' bread and eating it. But now, after it had been rebuked, it trembled and took hold of the hem of the elder's garment to pull him along.
Following it, he saw the watchman [?] at the top of the rock, rolled down among the crevices, and found him lying lifeless. He set the wolf free and commanded it:
"Do not be a cause of harm in this place any longer." These miracles last to this day, for the wild beasts of the field do no harm to the livestock.
He also performed many other miracles. After this he appointed Evagrius father of the monks, and he himself went down into a pit, a dark cave that no one could reach.
How could anyone describe his courage and endurance, his prayer, the way he bore the temptations of the demons, his tears and his supplication to the Lord?
There he brought his life to a good end. He asked for the holy sacrament from a priest and departed to the Lord, and he was received [into burial] in that very place
where he had completed his struggle. His tomb can be seen to this day, the hope of the Georgians.
Year after year relics spring up [?], strengthening the faithful and astonishing the unbelievers. While he was still alive, he performed many miracles:
he parted the great river Aragvi, made a lame man walk, made an angry king gentle, and healed one who was afflicted by unclean spirits;
he gave a child to a childless couple, and he made that son catholicos. His holy body was laid in the cave that had been his dwelling and the place of his struggle.
There was a holy father, Ise of Tsilkani, a disciple of the holy father John. We do not know his parents or his place of origin. We know only this:
he came with John, and under much pressure the catholicos of Kartli consecrated him bishop of the see of the holy Mother of God in the land of Mukhrani, in the village of Tsilkani.
Through his teaching he converted many unbelievers, and he spread instruction and preaching throughout his flock.
That village had lost hope because it had no water. The Ksani was far away, and a forest and a high hill lay in between.
One day he took up his staff after he had finished [the service] and offered supplication before the icon of the Mother of God. He came to the bank of the Ksani and commanded the water:
"By the power of our Lord Jesus Christ and of Mary the Mother of God, I command you, river: come out, follow in my footsteps, and go after the tip of my staff."
It followed him through a place where there was no path or road, going after him like a servant. He led it down to Tsilkani [?], where that water flows to this day.
After this he carried out many labors by the Lord's help, served out the office of bishop with joy, and committed his worthy, holy soul to God.
His all-honorable body was received in that same monastery of Tsilkani, where it can be seen to this day as a hope and a source of intercession for the Georgians.
Father Anthony of Mesopotamia was also a disciple of Father John. This saint was especially virtuous and distinguished among the hermits.
This all-blessed one [?] … the holy image of our Lord Jesus Christ, which He imprinted from His own face on a cloth, and so fulfilled Abgar's hope;
after the Ascension He sent it by the hand of Thaddeus and healed Abgar of the leprosy that afflicted him. Abgar was baptized with all his household by the hand of Thaddeus.
After him, the son of Abgar, and later the son of his grandson, succeeded them only in their kingship and not in their service of God.
For they had turned away from the service of God and become slaves to the wonders of demons.
For because of what Abgar had done to the demons, how he had shattered them and turned away from them, [one] of his [line] wished to take vengeance, so as to repay the demons
[for] the overthrow of that old sacrificial [idol] [?], by overthrowing the image of the Lord which Abgar had set up over the gates of the city, where there had stood
the foul idol. For there he had placed that image on cloth, stretched over a board, so that all who entered there might see it and worship it.
Then Abgar's foul grandson chose disgrace instead of prosperity, and renounced the image, and followed the demons, and plotted against that image of Christ, to destroy it.
Then the bishop of that city perceived the intention of that evil man, and made an arrangement worthy of and suited to that time.
For the place where the image had been set was made in the form of a vault, and the holy bishop placed a lit lamp there, as a covering [?] of that sanctuary;
he set up a tile in front of the image, and walled up the opening of the vault, and concealed it, so that it was not at all apparent that [?] one [thing] was nearer [?].

And afterwards, in later times, Khosrow, king of the Persians, besieged the city of Edessa, and began digging beneath the wall, and wished that they might enter that way, so that [the citizens] would not perceive that he was attacking.
Then God did not leave unfulfilled the unfailing promise that he had promised, namely:
"I am the wall of Edessa." And through the intercession of his Mother, the Mother of God appeared to Eulalius, the bishop of that city, and said:
"Over such-and-such a gate is that image not made by hands, and it is hidden."
And when the bishop awoke, he understood in truth the vision shown [to him] in [his sleep?] [text reads "in the throat"], and at dawn he went in procession with a litany to that place,
and found the holy image entirely undamaged, and the lamp before it had remained burning throughout so great a length of time;

and they poured the oil of that lamp down upon those who were fighting against the city, and immediately, as it reached them, it caught fire and they were burned, and they were scattered like dust and vanished.
And on the tile that had been set up as a covering for that image, another image had been imprinted, a likeness of that holy image of the Lord.
These were honoured equally, and they had been placed in the church of the Nestorians.
Then this holy Anthony sought out the way of his teacher, and learned the truth, and found out that he had gone to Armenia, to the northern region,
with the other disciples whom we have now mentioned, David, and Dodo, and Shio of Antioch, and eight other disciples of John, of the same region.
When holy Anthony learned this, he was stirred by love for his teacher; and this too was grievous to his heart,
that the images of the Lord were in the church of the Nestorians. And he took up the tile which had been the covering of that image, on which the image had been formed.
This he carried away unseen, led by an angel and by heavenly direction, to the north, and he reached the Mtkvari,
crossed it, and settled to the east, about four miles [away], in a cleft of the rock within the Akriani mountains.
He was about five miles from John, about nine miles from Shio, and thirteen miles from David and Dodo.
And there it was that deer would stand by this holy Anthony to nourish his body.
And the mountain was waterless and [?], and there was a small town about one mile [away].
And these deer would go out to the field, and when the time came they would come home for milking, as if shepherds
were bringing them at the proper hour. But once they arrived at an unusual time, frightened, and behind them followed a fawn whose flesh had been cut.
And the saint wondered at this and said in his heart: "Where has someone come upon them?"
For he did not know the surroundings [?] of that city, and at once, as men do with a dim-sighted glance [?], he said to them:
"What is that?" And they, as if they could speak, nodded their heads and said: "Follow me, and we will show you."
And he followed their tracks and came to the place where he had met them. And behold, the ruler of that village was coming to hunt, and he met him and said:
"Who are you?" But the saint showed with his hand where he lived and everything about his situation, for he did not understand the language. Then the ruler said:
"I do not understand your language, and that hand you are speaking to me with, I will cut it off as well." And he said: "Take him to the smith."
And when they had brought him, the smith heated an iron red-hot and took it out to cut off his hand, but he fell down, and his hands became like pieces of wood.
Then the saint stretched out his hand, and taking up the iron in his hand like a live coal, he held it out to him and said: "Do quickly what you were commanded."
And he was terrified at that dreadful sight. And they quickly informed the ruler and told him everything that had been seen.
And he ordered that he be brought before him. And when they had brought him, he said to him: "Say what you wish, and I will give you everything."
But he showed him a small stone, about [?] (samuli) in size, and licked it, and they understood that he wanted salt, and they brought him just two unbroken blocks.
And he broke off one litra and went away and gave it to his cows to lick. And he stayed before that icon until the end of his life.
And that saint passed away among the saints and left us that icon of the Lord, and it remains hidden to this very day,
and openly works miracles, so that it is easier to count the sands of the sea than the wonders of that icon of the Lord.
But since God alone is the worker of miracles, he alone knows the multitude of his miracles.
And even if it were Solomon, he could not count them; only God alone can.

1. The rebellion of the Khaskuns. At the time when the autocrat Justinian, king of the Greeks, was fighting in the regions of Ossetia, on the border of Abasgia, against the people of the Khaskuns, for they had rebelled,
then Justinian sent great gifts to Pharasmanes, king of the Georgians, and begged him to help his army with all his strength and make war on the Khaskuns.
So Pharasmanes heeded the request of the king of the Greeks, and left Evagrius as guardian of his kingdom, while he himself went out and, with God's help, subdued that people of the Khaskuns.
And he sent all their chiefs as captives to Justinian. Then he returned to his own kingdom.
2. The Fifth Ecumenical Council. In the twenty-sixth year of Justinian's reign the Fifth Council was held, of one hundred and sixty-five holy fathers, in the year 527 after Christ,
at Constantinople, under Vigilius, the holy pope of Rome; its presidents were Eutychius of Constantinople,
Apollinaris of Alexandria, Domnus of Antioch, and, standing in for the bishop of Jerusalem, the bishops Stephen, George and Damian.
And they assembled concerning the Origenists and those who followed them, Didymus and Evagrius, whom they anathematized and condemned.
3. The conversion of the Abkhazians. In those same times of Justinian's reign the Abkhazians also changed for the better and accepted the preaching of Christianity.
For in the palace of King Justinian there was a certain eunuch, an Abkhazian by birth, Euphratas by name, who was sent by the king to preach to them and to promise
that from then on not a single one of their nation would be deprived of his manhood by the knife.
For many of them were servants of the royal bedchamber, whom custom knows by the name of eunuch.
Therefore Justinian built a church of the holy Mother of God in Abkhazia, at Bichvinta, and appointed priests in it, so that they might teach the law of Christianity more openly.
But let us return to our earlier account. From the reign of King Mirian until that of the second Pharsman, two hundred and fifty years passed.
And fourteen kings passed away. And from Vakhtang's time eight catholicoi passed away. And Pharsman died, and his son Bakur took the throne as king.
The thirty-eighth king, Bakur, son of King Pharsman. This Bakur, of the Khosroid line, was a believer and a builder of churches.
He increased the number of churches and priests in his kingdom and cleansed Kartli of all unbelief.
And Catholicos Evlavios died, and that same king installed Makari as catholicos. At this same time there reigned in Persia one who was called Hormizd.
And at that same time there was in Armenia a man, a son of princes, named Vasken. And he had a wife, a daughter of princes, who was called Shushanik, the daughter of Vardan.
But the devil took hold of this Vasken, and he resolved to turn to fire-worship. He went before the king of the Persians, abandoned the faith of Christ, and became a fire-worshipper.
And the king of the Persians sent him back with great gifts as eristavi (governor) of Ran.
When he came back, and his wife Shushanik learned that her husband had abandoned the faith of Christ, she would no longer consent to be his wife.
And she forgot her love for her husband, and with all her heart she followed Christ, to fulfil his commandments.
Then Vasken pressed her in many ways: first with flattery and entreaty and the giving of gifts;
afterwards he cast her into great tortures, so that because of their length we cannot write down the struggles of the holy Shushanik.
And her husband Vasken, the eristavi of Ran, killed her.
Then Bakur, king of the Georgians, summoned all his eristavis, gathered troops in secret, and marched against Vasken by stealth.
For Vasken was camped out on the plain on the bank of the Kura, where the river of Anakerti joins the Kura. He fell upon him and seized Vasken.
They cut him into small pieces and hung his limbs on a tree. And the body of the holy Shushanik they carried away with great honour and buried at Tsortavi.
This King Bakur sent an envoy before the king of the Persians, informed him of all this, and asked his forgiveness.
Then the king of the Persians considered in his mind and said: "If I am angry with the Georgians, they will unite with the Greeks."
And he chose forgiveness. He sent back Bakur's envoy with a favourable answer, for he declared all the blame and guilt to be the slain Vasken's, and held Bakur justified in the killing [?]
[...] his. And he sent another eristavi, named Darel, to Ran and Movakan.
And he ordered him to keep good friendship with the Georgians. And the Catholicos Makari died, and that same king installed Svimon as catholicos.
And Bakur died, and his sons were left small children, who were unable to hold the kingship.
Then Hormizd, king of the Persians, gave Ran and Movakan to his son, whose name was Khosro Abarvez.
He came and settled at Bardav, and began to conspire with the eristavis of Kartli:
he promised them great benefits, and granted them in writing their eristavates as hereditary possessions from son to grandson, and so won them over with flattery.
And the eristavis rebelled, and each separately paid tribute to Khosro Abarvez. And the sons of Bakur remained in the mountain region of Kakheti;
and the descendants of Mirdat, son of Vakhtang, who ruled Klarjeti and Javakheti, remained among the rocky strongholds of Klarjeti.
All the rest of Kartli, Armenia and Vaspurakan the Persians seized, and they made war on the Greeks.
A few years after this, great disturbances arose in Persia, for the king of the Turks invaded Persia;
the Greeks came and engaged the Persians in Mesopotamia, routed them, entered Persia, and began to plunder Persia.
Then Khosro Abarvez abandoned Ran and Kartli and went to help his father.
When the Persians were thus occupied, all the eristavis of Kartli, upper and lower, conferred together and sent an envoy to the king of the Greeks,
and asked that he appoint for them a king from the line of the kings of Kartli, and that those eristavis remain each in his own eristavate without being removed.
Then the emperor granted their request, and gave them as king the sister's son of Mirdat, son of Vakhtang by his Greek wife; his name was Guaram, and he ruled Klarjeti and Javakheti.
The thirty-ninth king of Kartli: the kouropalates Guaram Bagrationi. This Guaram was a Khosroid on his mother's side and a Bagratid on his father's side.
And these Bagratids are the descendants and kin of this Guaram. The emperor granted this Guaram the title of kouropalates and sent him to Mtskheta.
And the sons of King Bakur, the kin of Dachi son of Vakhtang, to whom King Vakhtang had given the kingship, remained in Kakheti.
And they took possession of Kukheti and Hereti from the Iori onward, and settled at Ujarma, and were in submission to the kouropalates Guaram.
Then the emperor sent a great treasure with the kouropalates Guaram, and ordered him to use that treasure to bring out the armies of the North,
join the Georgian troops to them, and send them into Persia. And Guaram did so: he brought out the Ossetes,
the Durdzuks and the Didos, and put the eristavis of Kartli at their head. They entered Adarbadagan and began to plunder it.
And such hardships and troubles came upon the Persians. Then there appeared in Persia a man whose name was Bahram Chobin.
He engaged the Turks who had invaded Persia, as is clearly written in the History of the Persians; he killed Saba, king of the Turks, and routed their camp.
And the Greek troops that had entered Persia turned back and went home.
And those northerners whom Guaram the curopalates had sent also went back home.
For once the Persians were free of the Turks, they became afraid, and fear and trembling of the Persians fell upon the Georgians.
And this Guaram the curopalates began to fortify the fortresses and cities.
And again God showed mercy to the Christians, and another conflict broke out in Persia: for that same Bahram Chobin rebelled against the king of the Persians, and they put out
the eyes of King Hormizd, they being the brothers of his wife; and Chobin and Khosrow began to fight. Khosrow was driven out by Chobin and went to the land of the Greeks.
And the emperor Maurice gave his own daughter to Khosrow as wife, and gave him his army and sent him against Chobin.
Chobin was driven out of Persia, and Khosrow took control of Persia. Then the emperor Maurice took up the cause of the Georgians with Khosrow and said:
"Since the Georgians abandoned the service of idols, from that time on they have been subject to the Greeks;
for in the time of your tyranny Kartli was ruined, and otherwise [?] you have no rightful claim over Kartli.
Now, by the command of God, since you and I are in perfect love, let Kartli between us be independent, in peace:
I am the helper and protector of all the Georgians and of all Christians." Then the king of the Persians gave way to the emperor, and the Georgians were set free.
And this Guaram the curopalates remained in submission to the Greeks. He was a believing man and a builder of churches.
He began the church of the Precious Cross; until then the Cross had stood in the open field. And he built the church only up to waist height [?].
And he ruled well and without disturbance. But he could not remove the eristavis of Kartli from their eristavates,
for they held charters from the king of the Persians and from the king of the Greeks granting them hereditary possession of their eristavates; but they were in submission to Guaram the curopalates.
And this Guaram the curopalates had sons, of whom one was named Stephen and the other Demetrius.
And the catholicos Simon died, and Samuel took the seat. And the catholicos Samuel died, and they installed another Samuel.
This same Guaram the curopalates renewed the foundations of the Sioni of Tbilisi; after this Guaram they completed the building of the Sioni of Tbilisi:
half of it was built by a certain widowed woman, and half by all the people, in the time of the first prince Adarnase, and that Adarnase also helped with its construction.
For the descendants of the believing King Mirian were all builders of churches.
And Guaram the curopalates died. The fortieth chief of the eristavis of Kartli: Stephen, son of Guaram the curopalates, a Bagratid. And his son Stephen took the throne.
He did not dare take the title of king for fear of the Persians and the Greeks, but they called him chief of the eristavis.
And the catholicos Samuel died, and this Stephen installed Bartholomew as catholicos.
But this Stephen was unbelieving and without fear of God; he did not serve God, nor did he do anything to advance the faith or the churches.

And in his time a great upheaval took place in the land of the Greeks: for Phocas the soldier rebelled against the emperor Maurice, and killed the emperor Maurice and his children. And Phocas the soldier took control of the land of the Greeks.
Then the emperor's son-in-law, Khosrow, king of the Persians, set out to avenge the blood of his father-in-law and his brothers-in-law by invading and plundering the land of the Greeks.
He prevailed over the Greeks, and the emperor Phocas could not withstand him.
But Stephen, prince of Kartli, was afraid of the king of the Persians. He broke away from the Greeks and went over to the Persians.
At that time the same king Khosrow plundered Jerusalem and carried off the Wood of Life;
and after this God withdrew his hand of mercy from Khosrow: his own son seized him and put him in prison, and he died of a terrible disease.
In the time of this Stephen, Mtskheta was declining and Tbilisi was growing strong; Armazi was being laid waste and Kala was being built up.
And Stephen's brother, named Demetre, was building the church of the Holy Cross.
For he too had a terrible disease, and he could not leave the door of the church. Stephen ruled over all Kartli. He resided in Tbilisi, and he was subject to the Persians.
Some years after this a man appeared in the land of the Greeks, a kinsman of the emperor Maurice, named Heraclius.
He killed the emperor Phocas and took the land of the Greeks. He grew strong, brought the Turks from the west, and gathered
countless armies, and set out for Persia to seek the Wood of Life.
He came first to Kartli, to Samtskhe, and heard of the miracles worked by the icon on which the holy Mother of God had imprinted her image and which had been given for Andrew the First-Called,
who had brought it to rest and placed it in a small chapel at Atskuri. The emperor Heraclius came to see and venerate that icon.
Then Heraclius began to lay the foundation of a great church at Atskuri and to build it. Afterwards it was completed by faithful men, and after that they made it an episcopal see.
This Stephen did not want to break away from the Persians. He fortified his fortified towns and took up his position in Tbilisi. King Heraclius came and laid siege to Tbilisi.
Now Stephen was a brave and daring horseman. Every day he would come out of the city gates and fight the Greeks.
Then, in one of those battles, they threw Stephen down and killed him. And the emperor took Tbilisi.
But men stayed in the fortress of Kali and did not submit to the king; and from the fortress the commander of the fortress insulted the king and said:
"You have the beard of a goat and the neck of a young goat." Then the king said:
"Although this man called me a young goat to mock me, his words are not empty."
He took the book of Daniel and found this written in it: "A goat shall come out of the west and shall break the horns of the ram of the east."
Then the king rejoiced and took this as confirmation that he would be victorious over the Persians in everything.
Then the emperor summoned the son of Bakur, king of the Georgians, of the line of Dachi son of Vakhtang,
who was eristavi in Kakheti and whose name was Adarnase, and gave him Tbilisi and the rule of Kartli.
He left with him an eristavi named Jibgha and ordered him to make war on Kala, and the king himself set out to fight the Persians. The forty-first prince of Kartli: Adarnase.
Son of Bakur, a Khosroid. This Adarnase, prince of Kartli, and the eristavi Jibgha began to fight against the fortress of Kala.
And the Caesar set out for Baghdad. A few days later they took Kala and captured the commander of the fortress.
This eristavi first filled the commander's mouth with drachmas, saying, "Because the Caesar was delighted by your words."
After this he flayed him and sent the skin after the Caesar to Gardabani. He did this because of the man's insolence toward the king.
And by such a death Stephanoz and his servants perished.
God did this to that prince Stephanoz because he did not live trusting in God: he was hostile to the believers and made friends with the unbelievers.
Then the Greeks again took the border regions of Kartli: Speri and the far end of Klarjeti, the seacoast.
The sons of Stephanoz remained among the rocks of Klarjeti. Adarnase, son of Bakur, took the rest of Kartli as presiding prince, and he too did not dare to take the title of king.
Each of the eristavis kept his own eristavate without change, and they obeyed the presiding prince Adarnase.
And the Catholicos Bartholomew died, and this Adarnase appointed John as catholicos.
And they sent him to Antioch, and a monk with him, both as envoys and for consecration.
For it had been laid down that the catholicos was to be consecrated from Antioch, and no one was able any longer to travel the road to Antioch. Because of this the Georgians were greatly concerned.
In the days of Theophylact, patriarch of Antioch, they sent envoys, and they came before Theophylact, the patriarch of Antioch,
and told the blessed Theophylact that the Christians who live in the lands of the Georgians were in great distress,
for since the days of the blessed Anastasius, the priest-martyr, no consecration had taken place because of how hard the roads were.
So he held a general council and, by the council's deliberation, together with his archbishops, metropolitans and bishops, decided
that the bishops of the catholicos's own diocese should gather and consecrate the catholicos whenever one was needed:
whoever divine grace shows to them and whomever they choose, and who pleases the king and the bishops, and the people and the members of that church.

He drew up for them a written memorandum in his own name and in the name of the council gathered there. And he ordained one of the two monks sent to him, John by name, as their catholicos for that time.
In this council of Antioch the catholicos was honoured and freed from them. For he is no longer under the authority of the patriarchs, nor do they
consecrate him; instead his own bishops consecrate him. From then on it became known throughout the land that he had been freed at the council of Antioch.
Then John, bishop of the Goths, was sent to Kartli by his own flock and people,
and he received ordination at Mtskheta from John, catholicos of Kartli, because at that time the regions of Greece were in the grip of the heresy of fighting against icons.
Some time later the Catholicos John died in turn, and this same Adarnase appointed Babila.
And King Heraclius entered Persia, killed King Khosrow, took Baghdad, and brought back the Wood of Life.
He came back by way of Kartli again, in the seventh year after he had passed through.
And the church of the Honorable Cross and the Sioni of Tbilisi were completed by Adarnase, prince of Kartli.
Then King Heraclius carried off from Manglisi and from Erusheti the footboards
and the nails of our Lord Jesus Christ, which Constantine had given to Mirian.
Adarnase, prince of Kartli, was distressed, and he begged the emperor not to carry off those gifts from God.
The emperor did not listen to his plea and carried them off. In the time of this Adarnase three catholicoi died: John, Babila and Tabor.
Adarnase died, and his son Stephen took his place. The forty-second prince of Kartli: Stephen, son of Prince Adarnase.
This Khosroid Stephen was more faithful than all the kings and princes of Kartli. He purified the faith and built churches.
He put up walls around the church of the Honorable Cross and built halls. He ordained an assembly for every Friday, and all the bishops and priests of that region gather there, and

they are with the catholicos before the Honorable Cross. They celebrate each Friday like Good Friday. And at the catholicos's seat there are assemblies every Thursday, and they celebrate the holy Sioni
as on Holy Thursday, with the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ.
And at Mtskheta, at the bishop's seat, there was an assembly every Tuesday, with a commemoration of Stephen the Protomartyr and of all the martyrs
who had been martyred by that great power of the Persians, and of Abibos, bishop of Nekresi, who converted most of the mountain people east of the Aragvi.
And they laid his honored body at Mtskheta, at the bishop's seat, in the burial place of the bishops.
And on his feast, more than on any other feast, they gather and glorify God.
In those times Muhammad had appeared. He was of the lineage of Ishmael and was the teacher of the Saracens' religion, and he conquered all of Arabia and Yemen.
And he died, and Abu Bakr took his place and invaded Persia.
For since King Heraclius had invaded Persia, Persia had been ruined, and there was no longer anyone left in Persia to resist.
This Abu Bakr the Hagarene conquered Persia. He entered Baghdad, forced most of the people to give up fire worship, and converted them to the Saracen faith.
And he died, and Umar took his place, and he grew even stronger.
King Heraclius was told that the Hagarenes were invading Syria and Jazira, which is Mesopotamia.
And Heraclius went out to Palestine to fight them there. There was a certain monk there, a man of God, and he said to the king:
"Flee, for the Lord has given the East and the South to the Saracens," a name that translates as "Sarah's dogs."
And the astrologers and skilled soothsayers told King Heraclius the same thing that the monk had said.
King Heraclius built a pillar and wrote on it: "Peace be with you, Mesopotamia and Palestine, until seven sevens have passed."
As for the 'sevens': this is how the philosophers found the time set for the Saracens in the books of Hermes Trismegistus, and that time is two hundred and fifty years.
By the years of Alexander, it was nine hundred and twenty-seven years of Alexander before the appearance of Muhammad.

At that time all the noble families of the Greeks buried their treasures in the ground, so that when they came back they would find those treasures and would not have the trouble of carrying them away and bringing them back again.
And the emperor (Caesar) Heraclius went through by the road of Ran, and entered Kartli a second time. He said to the people of the Persians, who had fled there from the Saracens:
"If you know that your kingdom has come to an end, leave the north and come with us."
And they left this land and buried their treasures. Some went with him and some stayed, and they deposited the charters of every treasure-store.

And when they wrote the charter, they recorded their family and their land and set it down, so that when the Greeks came, they could use that charter to seek out their kinsmen and divide the land and the treasure among each of them.
The Catholicos Tabor died, and they installed Samuel as Catholicos. After this some years passed.
In the year 656 after Christ, the Sixth Council of 170 holy fathers took place in Constantinople, in the thirteenth year of the reign of Constantine Pogonatus,
who was the father of Justinian. Its presidents were the priests Theodore and George and the deacon John,
the legates of Agatho, pope of Rome, together with George of Constantinople and Theophanes of Antioch.
This council decreed the following about the holy church of Georgia, which is holy Mtskheta: that it should be equal in honour to the holy apostolic catholic churches, the patriarchal ones;
that the Catholicos of Kartli should be equal to the patriarchs; and that he should consecrate, shepherd and govern with righteousness the archbishops,
metropolitans and bishops, and his own flock: Kartli on this side and the far side, Kakheti, Shaki, Shirvan, and the mountain country adjoining and extending along it,
up to the border of Svaneti and Circassia, all of Ossetia, and all of Upper Kartli, Samtskhe-Saatabago.
"For this reason we have assigned the churches of Georgia to him. Let them serve him, be under his hand and obey his law,
and be shepherded by him. And we have given him the power of binding and loosing: whatever he binds, let it be bound in heaven;
and whatever he looses on earth, let it be loosed in heaven. From the beginning it was honoured by the Council of Antioch,
and by this council we have confirmed it as a patriarchate, so that no metropolitan or bishop may be made without the Catholicos's permission.
If anyone, whether an archbishop, a metropolitan or a bishop, dares to rise up against the Catholicos, or seizes a see and a church by force,
without asking the Catholicos and without his permission, or if a king or princes, or archbishops and metropolitan-bishops, are consecrated in this way, let them be cut off.
And whenever he wishes to prepare and consecrate the chrism, let him consecrate it in his own church."
For many people asked us many times about these matters, and in our ignorance we stumbled.
And like a gatherer of seed, we have collected these few words, which were scattered here and there in the holy writings, and brought them together at your command, O man of God.
Now Stephen had two sons, Archil and Mihr. And he divided up the whole treasury (khuastagi) of his kingdom, the treasure-store of gold and silver and precious stones:
He took half to the land of Egrisi, and he took with him his firstborn son Mihr. Half of his property he gave to Archil, his younger son. And Archil
buried the greater treasury in the gorge of Kakheti, and the vessels of gold and silver used in service in the gorge of Ujarma,
and he placed the treasuries of Kartli and Javakheti in a hill. That same Heraclius had appointed this hill as a hiding place for the treasures they could not carry away with them.
The name of that hill is Tontio, which in translation is "mountain of gold."
He set a talisman upon it, so that no one would be able to take the treasure out. And he buried the treasuries of all the churches of Kartli in the shadow of the great Sioni in Mtskheta.
After a short time Archil also went in, in the same way. While he was there, Stephen, the prince of Kartli, died, and in his place his son Mir became king.
The forty-third king: Mir, son of the prince Stephen, a Khosroid. For an Agarene emir came to Kartli, who was called Marwan the Deaf,
son of Muhammad. He had been sent by Hisham, the Commander of the Faithful in Baghdad, son of Abd al-Malik, of their kin.
He was given the second name "the Deaf" because he would not heed the words of counsellors.
When he took the rule of the Persians and Arabs, he stirred up every tribe and race of the Agarenes. He campaigned against the Christians, laid waste and slaughtered, and took captive the land

of Greece and of Armenia as far as the sea. He spread over the northern regions like a cloud of darkness, as many as locusts and [?] (mumli, a kind of locust or insect swarm), and covered the face of the earth.
All the princes and patiakhshes, the kin of the eristavs and of the nobles, fled to the Caucasus and hid in the forests and ravines.
The Deaf went through all the Caucasus. He seized the Gate of Darial and the Gate of Derbent, and destroyed all the cities and most of the fortresses within all the borders of Kartli.
He came to Samtskhe and camped in the region of Odzrkhe, for that city was famous at that time because of its ancient deeds.
Then he set out, came out of Samtskhe and headed for the land of Argveti, and the vanguard and the picked troops went ahead.
At that time there were two great princes, glorious by lineage, Georgians from the districts of the land of Argveti: David and Constantine.
They were then gathered together, picked men, and on their guard. When the heathen saw David and Constantine, they roared like beasts and attacked them.

But David strengthened his band and made them fearless. He roared like a lion, routed the enemy and scattered them. They slaughtered countless numbers of them, and he raised up victory for the Christians.
Then the fugitives turned back and told Marwan the Deaf what had happened to them: that the wood-worshippers had slaughtered all the picked troops of the vanguard.
